## README (README.md)

# Beatboxing to MIDI (Frozen In Flames Edition)

A static web application that transcribes a beatbox recording into programmed MIDI. Onset detection and classification separate the performance into its constituent sound types (kick, snare, hat, bass, hum, and effects), and the result is exported as one Standard MIDI File per sound type together with a combined master file. Execution is entirely in the browser: no backend and no build step.

## Live demonstration

- [Beatboxing to MIDI](https://frozen-in-flames.github.io/beatboxing-to-midi/): the full application, running in the browser.

## Authorship and version history

## Authorship and version history

Beatboxing to MIDI (Frozen In Flames Edition) was created, designed, and built by Aries Hilton (Frozen In Flames). It is an original work: the onset detection, classification, calibration, layer separation, and MIDI export pipeline was designed and shipped by its author before any third-party transcription component was involved in it.

Dated record:
- v1.0.0, October 2026: first public release.
- v1.0.1, October 2026: built-in classifier retrained on real labeled audio (the AVP dataset, CC-BY-4.0), scoring 60.3% on voices never heard in training.
- v1.0.2, October 2026: the first personal model, trained only on the creator's own voice recordings. The recordings themselves ship in `dataset/` with the audit manifest in `PROVENANCE.md`, so the weights can be traced back to the exact audio they were trained on

chunks.h: Beatboxing to MIDI (Frozen In Flames Edition) > Authorship and version history
chunks.t:
with the audit manifest in `PROVENANCE.md`, so the weights can be traced back to the exact audio they were trained on

.
- v1.0.3, October 2026: the Basic Pitch pitched layer. Spotify's Basic Pitch (Apache License 2.0, Copyright 2022 Spotify AB; see `NOTICE.md`) is incorporated as a credited third-party component that proposes sustained bass and hum notes when the user enables "Enhanced pitch". The creator's own pitch tracker keeps pitch bends and glides, and both drum models are unchanged. The component was benchmarked against the existing pipeline before it was incorporated (2026-10-23) and admitted only where it measured better.

## What it does

- Record from the mic (browser voice processing switched off, since it smears hats) or open an audio file.
- Onset detection (spectral flux) finds each sound; per-event features and YIN pitch describe it.
- Classification three ways, in order

chunks.h: Beatboxing to MIDI (Frozen In Flames Edition) > What it does
chunks.t:
(spectral flux) finds each sound; per-event features and YIN pitch describe it.
- Classification three ways, in order

: your own calibration samples (nearest neighbour), the active built-in model, or built-in rules. Two built-in models ship with the app, and a picker in the Convert section chooses between them: the general model (`model/model.json`) and the Aries personal model (`model/model-aries.json`).
- Layer separation (HPSS) splits a clip into a harmonic layer and a percussive layer, so a hum under hats is tracked as pitch while the hats are detected as drums.
- Enhanced pitch (optional, online): with layer separation on, an "Enhanced pitch" toggle brings in the Basic Pitch model to propose sustained bass and hum notes. It loads on demand at convert time and changes nothing unless you turn it on. Pitch bends and glides still come from the built-in tracker. See the Enhanced pitch s

chunks.h: Beatboxing to MIDI (Frozen In Flames Edition) > What it does
chunks.t:
nothing unless you turn it on. Pitch bends and glides still come from the built-in tracker. See the Enhanced pitch s

ection below.
- Pitch bends: a pitch jump over 1 semitone starts a new note; smaller movement stays one note with pitch-bend points (bend range 12 semitones).
- Tempo is detected from the onsets when the Tempo box is left blank, and can snap events to 16th notes.
- Unknown SFX are clustered by timbre into `sfx1`, `sfx2`, and so on, each with its own MIDI note and file. Name a cluster in the page and those sounds become calibration samples and the conversion reruns.
- Drums use General MIDI notes on channel 10. Bass and hum use the detected pitch. Velocity comes from event loudness.

## Run it online

Push to GitHub, then Settings > Pages > deploy from the main branch. `index.html` at the repo root loads `src/app.js`; no build step.

## Run it offline

Download `dist/beatboxing-to-midi-offline.zip` (or zip this repo yourself), unzip it, serve the folder locally, and open it in a browser:

```
cd beatboxing-to-midi-offline
python3 -m http.server

# open http://localhost:8000

```

A local server is required because browsers will not load ES modules from `file://`. By default the app makes no external network requests; the only files it fetches are the classifier model files next to it. The one exception is the Enhanced pitch toggle (online use only): enabling it fetches ONNX Runtime Web from a CDN plus the Basic Pitch model served with the page. In the offline package the toggle simply reports itself unavailable and the built-in pitch tracker is used. See `OFFLINE.md` in the zip for details.

## Built-in models and measured accuracy

Two trained models ship with the app. The picker in the Convert section chooses which one labels your sounds, and the page states which is active. Your own calibration, when present, overrides both. The general model is the default, for the measured reason in the personal model section below: the personal model wins on its own voice and loses on everyone else's, so it is offered as a labeled choice, never swapped in silently.

### General model (v1.0.1, `model/model.json`)

Trained on real labeled beatbox audio, not synthetic examples. Accuracy was measured two ways; both numbers are reported because they answer different questions:

chunks.h: open http://localhost:8000 > Built-in models and measured accuracy > General model (v1.0.1, `model/model.json`)
chunks.t:
synthetic examples. Accuracy was measured two ways; both numbers are reported because they answer different questions:

- **Voices the model never heard** (trained on 20 of 25 people, graded on the 5 unseen ones): **60.3% overall** (kick 76.0%, snare 41.7%, hat 61.2%). This is the honest estimate for a brand-new user.
- **Benchmark protocol on the shipped code** (graded on full improvisation takes; those voices were in the training data, the performances were not): **71.9%**.
- **Your own calibration still wins**: teaching it 5 samples per sound scores 74.5% on the same benchmark, so calibrating with your own voice remains the most accurate path.

Full method, confusion counts, and limits: `docs/training-avp.md`.

chunks.t:

Full method, confusion counts, and limits: `docs/training-avp.md`.

> The built-in classifier weights in `model/model.json` were trained on the Amateur Vocal Percussion (AVP) dataset by Delgado et al. (2019), available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3250230 under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license (CC-BY-4.0). The dataset provided the kick, snare, and hat training audio; the bass and hum classes were trained on synthetic examples generated for this project. No AVP audio files are distributed with this project; only the trained weights derived from them.

### Personal model (v1.0.2, `model/model-aries.json`)

Trained only on the creator's own voice: 1,092 sounds segmented from the 10 studio stems in `dataset/` (479 s of audio, recorded dry on October 23, 2026, no presets, no autotune). No other voice, no other dataset, and no synthetic example is in it. The full audit chain from recordings to weights is in `PROVENANCE.md`; the full training record is `docs/training-aries.md`.

- **On his held-out sounds** (trained on 80% of the segmented events, graded on the unseen 20%): **62.4% overall** (hat 74.3%, sfx 71.0%, hum 66.7%, kick 53.1%, snare 53.1%, bass 51.3%). The caveat matters: held-out here means unseen events from the same recording session. It is not the same kind of held-out as the general model's unseen-voices figure, and the two numbers should not be read as a head-to

-head.
- **The general model grading his sounds on the same held-out events: 39.6%**, and his bass scores **0.0%** (0 of 39). The general model's bass class was trained on synthetic tones; his real vocal bass is a different physical sound, and it reads as kick and hat to that model. The personal model exists because of gaps like this.
- **The tradeoff runs both ways**: the personal model scores **34.1%** on the AVP voices (against the general model's 60.3% participant-held-out there). A model of one mouth is a model of one mouth.
- **Calibration note**: on the creator's own data, few-sample calibration tops out at 49.3% (10 samples per class; 41.6% at 3 and at 5 per class), below the trained personal model's 62.4%. The usual advice that calibration wins was measured on

## Enhanced pitch (v1.0.3, optional, online)

The built-in pitch tracker (YIN over the HPSS harmonic layer) is good at bends and glides and weak at one measured thing: sustained vocal bass. On the creator's own 56 s bass stem it recovered 10 notes covering 1.5 s; the rest failed its clarity gate, because his bass is a pulse-like sound, not a clean tone. Basic Pitch, a transcription model built for sustained pitched notes, recovered the line. v1.0.3 therefore splits the pitched layer by measured strength:

chunks.h: open http://localhost:8000 > Enhanced pitch (v1.0.3, optional, online)
chunks.t:
built for sustained pitched notes, recovered the line. v1.0.3 therefore splits the pitched layer by measured strength:

- **Basic Pitch proposes sustained pitched events** (onset, offset, pitch) when you enable the "Enhanced pitch" toggle. It reads the raw clip, no HPSS needed.
- **The built-in tracker keeps pitch bends and glides.** A note whose bend contour travels (a glide) is kept exactly as the built-in tracker wrote it, and Basic Pitch proposals overlapping it are dropped. Where the two agree on a note, the built-in version wins, because its bend contour is continuous where the model's is stepped.
- **Harmonic-companion suppression.** A voice's upper partials make the model report extra simultaneous notes at harmonic positions of a stronger fundamental; left in, they write a second, wrong melody line into the MIDI. A filter in `src/basicpitch.js` suppresses a note when a strictly s

chunks.h: open http://localhost:8000 > Enhanced pitch (v1.0.3, optional, online)
chunks.t:
write a second, wrong melody line into the MIDI. A filter in `src/basicpitch.js` suppresses a note when a strictly s

tronger note overlaps it in time and it sits within 1 semitone of a harmonic (2nd to 16th) of that stronger note. Measured on the creator's stems, simultaneous harmonic companions went from 2 to 0 (bass), 25 to 0 (hum), and 18 to 0 (throat), at a cost of 2, 25, and 18 notes respectively: bass kept 65 of 67 notes, hum 99 of 124, throat 54 of 72.
- **Thresholds.** The model runs at its library default thresholds (onset 0.5, frame 0.3, minimum note length 127.70 ms), chosen by measurement: on the drums-only negative control (83.6 s of AVP improvisations and hat clicks, where every pitched note is a hallucination), the tuned configuration produces 22 phantom notes, 0.263 per second, at the benched untuned level (0.28/s) and well under the built-in layer's 0.66/s. Every strict

Measured on the creator's stems, app path, enhanced pitch on: the bass stem yields 65 pitched events covering 16.5 s (the built-in tracker alone: 10 notes); the hum stem 92 pitched events (built-in: 127 notes, cleaner in key but more fragmented); the throat-singing stem 55 (built-in: 85, fragmented). ## Teach it your sounds (calibration)

Record yourself repeating one sound, pick its name, then "Add clip as samples". Five or more repeats per sound works best. Calibration takes over once it covers at least two different sound types with at least three samples total; until then the trained model or the built-in rules do the labelling. Samples live in your browser's localStorage.

## Train a model

Put labelled WAV files in `data/<label>/` (for example `data/kick/*.wav`, 16-bit PCM) and run:

```
npm run train
```

chunks.h: open http://localhost:8000 > Train a model
chunks.t:
labelled WAV files in `data/<label>/` (for example `data/kick/*.wav`, 16-bit PCM) and run:

```
npm run train
```

The script prints training and held-out accuracy and writes `model/model.json`. Commit that file and the app uses it automatically whenever you have not calibrated. Check the licence of any dataset you train on before publishing a model trained on it: public vocal-percussion datasets can supply the audio, but their licences vary.

The `dataset/` folder in this repo is a worked example of a fully published training set: the personal model's audio, the label and key/BPM ground truth for every stem, and a SHA-256 provenance manifest ship together, so anyone can retrain from the same files and compare the resulting weights.

## How it works

A beatbox is one mouth on one channel, so there are no stems to separate. The app finds each sound and classifies it:

chunks.h: open http://localhost:8000 > How it works
chunks.t:
beatbox is one mouth on one channel, so there are no stems to separate. The app finds each sound and classifies it:

1. `src/dsp.js` detects onsets (spectral flux) and measures each sound: spectral centroid, low and high energy, zero crossings, decay length, and pitch (YIN). It also estimates tempo from onset times.
2. `src/layers.js` splits layers (median-filter HPSS) and tracks pitch contours into notes with bends.
3. `src/basicpitch.js` (only when Enhanced pitch is on) runs the Basic Pitch model and decodes its output into sustained pitched-event proposals, with the harmonic-companion filter applied. `src/pitchlayer.js` merges those proposals with the built-in tracker's notes under the boundary described above.
4. `src/classify.js` labels each sound (rules, trained model, or calibration k-NN), and `src/model.js` holds the shared math: z-scoring, k-means for SFX clusters, and the small

chunks.h: open http://localhost:8000 > How it works
chunks.t:
or calibration k-NN), and `src/model.js` holds the shared math: z-scoring, k-means for SFX clusters, and the small

 neural net the trained model uses.
5. `src/midi.js` writes standard MIDI files (format 1, one track per class plus a master).

## Limits

- Snare is the weak class, and the limit is the feature space, not the tuning: the general model fits snare at only 40% even on its own training data, because amateur "pf" snares genuinely overlap hats and kicks in the measured features. Per-user calibration (74.5% on the benchmark) is the current best fix for the general model. The personal model's held-out snare is 53.1% on the creator's voice (up from 41.7% for the general model on unseen voices, and 28.1% for the general model grading his snares), and it is still the weakest drum class: his snare subtypes measure as two opposed families, one kick-like and one hat-like, so the class c

chunks.h: open http://localhost:8000 > Limits
chunks.t:
weakest drum class: his snare subtypes measure as two opposed families, one kick-like and one hat-like, so the class c

onfuses in both directions.
- Bass and hum ground truth depends on the model. The general model's bass and hum classes rest on synthetic training examples (the AVP dataset contains none), verified by the ground-truth clips in `VERIFY.md` rather than graded real audio. The personal model's bass and hum are trained on real labeled recordings, of exactly one voice.
- Personal model scope: one voice, one session. Its 62.4% held-out figure grades unseen events from the same recordings it trained on; a different day or room is expected to score lower, and other voices score much lower (34.1% on the AVP voices). A second-session validation does not exist yet.
- The personal model's sfx class is a mixed bucket by design: it holds his clicks and his signature sounds, which is wh

- Layer separation (HPSS) is slow on long clips, so keep clips under about 30 s.
- A glide inside one note is written as pitch-bend points; a pitch jump over 1 semitone starts a new note.
- Tempo detection reads a uniform 8th-note grid at slow tempos as double tempo (a uniform grid carries no accent information to tell the two apart). Quarter-note patterns are detected exactly.
- Unknown sounds that sit inside a known class's feature range (for example a soft noise burst among snares) are labelled as that class; clearly distinct timbres are the ones that reach the SFX clusters.
- Calibration samples live in your browser's localStorage.
- Enhanced pitch needs an internet connection and downloads about 4 M

samples live in your browser's localStorage.
- Enhanced pitch needs an internet connection and downloads about 4 M

B of runtime the first time it is used in a session. It is off by default and the offline package does not include it.

# Beatboxing to MIDI: Aries voice-only retrain (candidate v1.0.2) + Basic Pitch real-voice exam

Date: 2026-10-23. Scope: train a personal model on Aries Hilton's own studio
recordings **only**, grade it honestly, cross-check it against the shipped
AVP-trained model in both directions, and run the Basic Pitch gate-2 exam on
his real pitched voice. This document is the training record for the v1.0.2
release: the weights it recommends shipped as `model/model-aries.json`, and
the recordings it grades ship in `dataset/` with `PROVENANCE.md`.

chunks.h: Beatboxing to MIDI: Aries voice-only retrain (candidate v1.0.2) + Basic Pitch real-voice exam
chunks.t:
recommends shipped as `model/model-aries.json`, and
the recordings it grades ship in `dataset/` with `PROVENANCE.md`.

All training/eval reuses the shipped code paths — `analyze()` / `vec()` from
`src/dsp.js` + `src/classify.js`, the MLP and recipe of `train/train.mjs`
(H=16, 400 epochs, seeded LCG, z-scored 6-feature vectors) — exactly as the
AVP training did. Scripts and raw output: `work/ingest.mjs`,
`work/train-aries.mjs`, `work/train-results.json`, `work/audit.json`.

labels and key/BPM are his ground truth from the session. Stereo was
downmixed to mono (channel mean) at ingest — the pipeline is mono by design.
(Contrast: `train.mjs`'s own WAV reader would silently have taken the left
channel only.)

120 bpm land at 2.8–3.6 events/s (beats plus subdivisions plus the detector's
known ~1.3 splits-per-onset behavior from the AVP extraction), pitched stems

of any class (0.501), throat and hum are the only high-clarity (voiced)
classes (0.702 / 0.559). *The low "mean pitch" figures for bass and lip roll

**Class mapping (explicit decision).** The app has no click or lip-roll
class, and a single hat class. Two label spaces were trained:

chunks.h: Beatboxing to MIDI: Aries voice-only retrain (candidate v1.0.2) + Basic Pitch real-voice exam > 1. Dataset inventory
chunks.t:
(explicit decision).** The app has no click or lip-roll
class, and a single hat class. Two label spaces were trained:

- **Native (10 classes):** bass, click, hat_closed, hat_open, hum, kick,
  liproll, sfx, snare, throat — his taxonomy as recorded.
- **Collapsed (6 classes, the candidate architecture):** labels
  `[bass, hat, hum, kick, snare, sfx]` — exactly `CLASSES` in
  `src/classify.js`. Mapping: closed + open hat → hat (mirrors the AVP
  treatment); lip roll → bass (it is a pitched sub-bass technique, in C
  minor, with the lowest spectral profile in the set); throat → hum (a
  sustained voiced sound; its clarity 0.702 groups it with hum's 0.559,
  not with the bass stem's pulse-like 0.009); click → sfx (clicks are NOT
  hat-like — mean high-band energy 0.077 vs closed hat's 0.958 — and sfx is

## 5. Basic Pitch real-voice exam (gate 2)

Method: both pitched engines ran on identical mono downmixes of his three
pitched stems. Basic Pitch via the bench's ONNX route (library defaults);
the incumbent via the app's own layers path (HPSS → `pitchNotes` YIN
contour). Ground truth is key-level only — C natural minor collection
{C D Eb F G Ab Bb} for hum and bass, chromatic for throat — because no
per-note transcription of his performance exists. Pitch-class-in-collection
is therefore a proxy: it cannot fully separate a performer playing outside
the collection from a tracker misreading. Where both systems independently
produce the same "out-of-scale" pitch classes in near-identical counts,
the evidence points at the source (performance chromaticism and harmonic
content), not at one tracker hallucinating alone. Reported with that limit
attached.

**SHIP — as the Aries personal model, labeled as such; do NOT silently
replace the AVP model as the universal default.**

- For the product's actual story — *his* software, *his* voice — the

## Label coverage: why bass and hum are in a "real data" model

Read of `src/classify.js`: when a model is loaded and the user has calibrated
fewer than two sound types, **every** event is classified by
`predict(model, ...)`. The model's label list is therefore the app's whole
label space in that mode. A model trained only on AVP drums would have made
bass and hum unreachable without calibration, breaking the non-layered
bass/hum path the shipped app has today. So the real model keeps the shipped
label set exactly: AVP provides real kick/snare/hat, and bass/hum rows are
the scaffold's existing synthetic training files (the same ones the shipped
model learned those classes from). SFX is unaffected either way: no model
label produces it, and its clustering path is unchanged.

## The final model (now the committed `model/model.json`)

Trained with recipe A on **all** 25 participants plus the synthetic bass/hum
rows (3,818 rows). Fit on its own training data, reported as fit and nothing
more: **66.9% overall** (kick 76.6%, snare 40.0%, hat 74.9%, bass 95%,
hum 95%). Training fit sitting close to the held-out score says the gap is
not overfitting; see the snare note under Limits.

chunks.t:
# collaborative-midi

- Repository: collaborative-midi
- Description: A collaborative MIDI editor with a conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) at its core: multiple peers edit one pattern concurrently over WebRTC data channels, with Standard MIDI File import and export. A single web page; no server and no account.
- URL: https://github.com/Frozen-In-Flames/collaborative-midi
- Primary language: JavaScript
- Last push: 2026-11-16T19:39:53Z

## README (README.md)

# Collaborative MIDI

Two or more people edit the same MIDI pattern live, at the same time, on one web page. The connection is direct between browsers: no server holds the session, no account, nothing to install. When the pattern sounds right, anyone in the session can export a Standard MIDI File that opens in any DAW.

## Live demonstration

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > Live demonstration
chunks.t:
sounds right, anyone in the session can export a Standard MIDI File that opens in any DAW.

## Live demonstration

- [Collaborative MIDI](https://frozen-in-flames.github.io/collaborative-midi/): the full application, running in the browser. Open it in two browsers or devices to rehearse the two-peer case.

## Why this exists

Making music together usually means sending files back and forth, or everyone buying into the same platform and its accounts. This page takes the opposite route, the one this whole portfolio is built on: open standards first, one web build, inherit the ecosystem. MIDI carries the music, WebRTC carries the session, Web Audio carries the sound, and a small conflict-free replicated document carries everyone's edits at once. One build runs everywhere a browser runs.

## How it works

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > How it works
chunks.t:
replicated document carries everyone's edits at once. One build runs everywhere a browser runs.

## How it works

- **The document.** A pattern is a set of notes: pitch, start, duration, velocity, channel, each with a stable id. Every edit is an operation stamped with the pair [lamport clock, peerId]. Any set of operations, applied in any order, with any duplication, lands every participant on the identical pattern. The math guarantees it; the test suite proves it a thousand times per gate run.
- **One format rule.** The pattern JSON this page saves is the CRDT document itself. The same data that syncs is the data you keep, share, and reopen. There is no internal format and no export translation to drift apart.
- **Connecting.** The host creates an offer code, the guest answers it, and the two browsers connect directly over an ordered WebRTC data channel. Codes are compressed and pasted

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > How it works
chunks.t:
answers it, and the two browsers connect directly over an ordered WebRTC data channel. Codes are compressed and pasted 

through any chat you already use. On connect, both sides exchange a version and lamport summary, then full state, then any delta ops the other is missing, then live edits as they happen.
- **Honest limits.** Connections use direct browser networking with no relay server, so the same network and most home networks connect easily, while some strict networks may block a direct connection. When a connect code is short enough, the page also shows it as a QR code. Real offer codes run about 700 characters, longer than a single QR code holds (586 bytes at the largest size this encoder supports), so for real sessions the text code is the path. Nothing is ever shortened or cut to force a fit.

## Editing

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > Editing
chunks.t:

## Editing

Click an empty cell to add a note. Drag a note to move it, drag its right edge to resize it, right-click to delete it. Two lanes: melody on channel 1, drums on channel 10, the General MIDI drum channel. Playback uses Web Audio lookahead scheduling (a 25 ms timer scheduling 100 ms ahead against the audio clock), so timing stays steady even when the tab is busy. Import a .mid file to keep working on it together; export a .mid to take the session anywhere.

## MIDI files

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > MIDI files
chunks.t:
is busy. Import a .mid file to keep working on it together; export a .mid to take the session anywhere.

## MIDI files

Files are written and read by code in this repo, from scratch: Standard MIDI File format 1, PPQ 480, drums on channel 10. That matches the conventions of the Frozen In Flames beatboxing-to-MIDI releases, so files move between the tools in this family without translation surprises. A round-trip test holds the line: export, re-import, and the note set must come back identical.

## Design decisions worth knowing

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > Design decisions worth knowing
chunks.t:
test holds the line: export, re-import, and the note set must come back identical.

## Design decisions worth knowing

- **Tombstones stay.** Deleting a note marks it dead and keeps the record. There is no tombstone garbage collection in this version, on purpose: collection is only safe once every peer has acknowledged a deletion, and sessions started by pasting codes cannot prove that. Pattern documents are small. Retention is cheap. Correctness is not negotiable.
- **Wall clocks never order anything.** Ordering is the [lamport, peerId] pair, with an explicit receive rule: on receiving an op, the local clock advances to max(local, remote) + 1. Device clocks lie; the pair does not.
- **Zero dependencies.** The core, the MIDI file code, the sync layer, and the QR encoder are all written in this repo. The page you open is the whole product, and it works offline as a solo editor with no connection at all.

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > Where the pattern came from
chunks.t:
in this repo. The page you open is the whole product, and it works offline as a solo editor with no connection at all.

## Where the pattern came from

This build is the third door of a standards-first doctrine. The first two doors are proven in this same body of work: Standard MIDI Files plus a browser page for instruments, and GeoJSON plus a browser page for city data. The doctrine was put to the general Meta AI model, and the model returned a third instance on its own: a collaborative tool, built from CRDTs plus WebRTC plus a web page. This repository is that returned pattern, built out and tested. The MIDI handling descends from the beatboxing-to-MIDI releases: same file format, same division, same drum channel, so the ecosystem stays one ecosystem.

## Tests

```
npm test     # unit suites: CRDT core, MIDI round trip, QR vectors
npm run oracle   # the convergence gate
```

chunks.h: Collaborative MIDI > Tests
chunks.t:
test     # unit suites: CRDT core, MIDI round trip, QR vectors
npm run oracle   # the convergence gate
```

The convergence oracle runs 1,000 iterations of a partition scenario: three peers, 50 seeded operations each round, edits made while partitioned, withheld operations queued and delivered in random order at full sync, and every final state required byte-equal over a canonical serialization. Its negative control runs the same scripts through a naive last-write-wins sync, which must diverge in at least 90% of runs, or the harness itself is judged broken. Current status: 1,000 of 1,000 converged, naive sync diverged in 100.0% of runs.

# DeadRamp Base

A walkable 3D twin of the FedRAMP Marketplace, generated from the
DeadRamp catalog: 674 vendor buildings and 781 service offerings laid
out on one spiral, in a single federal architectural language, that you
walk through in first person. It is a place, not a data viewer with
walls: movement, light, and scale are the interface, and the
architecture itself is the first read (who does what, at what tier, in
what state) before any sign is read.

> Clean-room model built from public FedRAMP Marketplace information,
> inspired by the vendor's public brand identity. Not affiliated with
> or endorsed by the vendor.

chunks.h: DeadRamp Base

information,
> inspired by the vendor's public brand identity. Not affiliated with
> or endorsed by the vendor.

That framing is the label. Inside the experience it lives in one
place only: the Settings panel (the button beside the help button),
under "About this model"; it is not repeated on walls, panels,
cards, or signs. It is carried here as repository documentation.
DeadRamp Base is a clean-room rebuild by Frozen In Flames. Vendor names are used nominatively and factually, from the
public Marketplace record, to identify whose services are modeled.
Colour schemes are evocation only: no logos, logotypes, wordmarks,
brand fonts, mascots, or trade dress elements are reproduced.

function, tier, status, and data, modeled faithfully from the public
record, and proven equivalent by the fidelity tests), different label
and packaging (our federal rendition), and a label that states plainly
it is not the brand product.

# DeadRamp Base: Plan (draft, Nov 14, 2026)

Status: brainstorm and plan, at Aries's direction. Build sequence: after fif-ears ships. Nothing here is built yet. This file is uncommitted working state in the deadramp repo.

## The idea in one line

DeadRamp stops being only text: the whole marketplace becomes a walkable VR base, generated from the repo's own data, where every vendor is a building and every service is a room you can stand inside.

## Ground truth it is generated from (measured Nov 14, 2026)

## Ground truth it is generated from (measured Nov 14, 2026)

- `forks.json` registry: 781 offerings, 674 distinct vendors.
- 101 group directories on two axes: function (accounting, ai, cybersecurity, cloud-infrastructure-hosting, collaboration, crm, data-management, development-tools, and the rest) crossed with trust tier (L1, L2, L3, untiered).
- Impact levels: Moderate 450, High 124, Low 24, LI-SaaS 42, Unknown 141.
- Authorization status: FedRAMP Certified 547; pipeline states 234 (Initial Implementation 102, Legacy Ready 53, Agency In Process 46, FedRAMP In Process 33).
- Built state: 779 of 781 offerings built; 2 honestly unclassified (TERIDA CLASsoft, USDA vGov). 40 gap entries re-scoped to the platform layer under PLATFORM-LAYER.md; union merges carry parent lineage.

USDA vGov). 40 gap entries re-scoped to the platform layer under PLATFORM-LAYER.md; union merges carry parent lineage.

The Base is a VIEW over this data, never a second source of truth. When the catalog changes, the Base regenerates.

## Layout law: one spiral, at every scale

Design reference (Aries, Nov 14, 2026): the worlds of Skyrim, Oblivion, and Dragon Age 2, where travel distance is governed by winding paths at every size, so a compact world feels vast. His words: things are a distance of a spiral no matter how close or far, small or large, it is all spirals. The spiral is therefore scale-invariant in the Base, not just the street plan:

- World scale: a single spiral boulevard is the whole map. Districts (the function groups) are placed in order along the spiral; inside a district, vendor buildings line the boulevard in registry order.

# DeadRamp Base v0.5.0: the accessibility release

This release implements the findings of the measured accessibility audit conducted against v0.4.0 (36 WCAG 2.2 criteria assessed: 21 pass, 12 fail, 3 not applicable, with three blockers). The Base is generated from data, so every fact in the scene can also exist as text; this release builds that second, fully equivalent surface and repairs the interaction defects the audit measured.

## What is new

chunks.t:
builds that second, fully equivalent surface and repairs the interaction defects the audit measured.

## What is new

**Directory mode.** A Directory button (and a skip link) opens a searchable, screen-reader-native directory rendered as real document structure: 81 district sections, all 674 vendors with their status stated in the same plain words the record cards use, and all 781 offerings with their launch modes. Each vendor offers Open record, Go to, and Enter building; inside a building, the Directory lists the rooms with Go to room and Open terminal actions. The directory is a pure function of the same catalog the scene renders from, so the text cannot drift from the place.

chunks.h: DeadRamp Base v0.5.0: the accessibility release > What is new
chunks.t:
The directory is a pure function of the same catalog the scene renders from, so the text cannot drift from the place.

**Full keyboard operation.** Turning takes the Comma and Period keys (the E key keeps its established action meaning: enter, launch, exit), and Enter performs the same centre pick a pointer click performs, opening the same cards and terminals. Touch visitors gain hold-to-turn pads. A keyboard-controls switch in Settings turns the scene keys off entirely.

**Announcements and focus care.** A polite live region announces arrival, district changes, door prompts, record opens, building entries and exits, and floor changes; terminal output is a live log. Opening any panel moves focus into it; closing returns focus to the control that opened it; Escape closes the topmost panel.

chunks.t:
any panel moves focus into it; closing returns focus to the control that opened it; Escape closes the topmost panel.

**Measured repairs.** Label fade floors are raised so vendor and district labels meet the 4.5:1 contrast requirement at rendered opacity (sampled 7.96:1 to 13.93:1; the same computation at the old floor fails at 4.12:1, which is the audit's defect reproduced as a negative control). The viewport no longer bans pinch zoom. All close buttons meet the 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum target size. The pooled scene labels are hidden from assistive technology, with their information carried by the Directory and announcements. The reduced-motion preference is honoured: under it, help does not fade and interior idle animation holds still.

**Comfort settings.** Settings gains reduced motion (following the operating system until set), high-contrast labels, larger labels, and the keyboard-controls switch, persisted across visits, plus an Accessibility statement that names what the environment provides and its remaining limits.

## Why

A public environment that can only be used with a pointer and a screen excludes visitors by construction. Because the Base is a generated view over a verified catalog, accessibility here is not an overlay: the same record that builds a building also builds its text equivalent, and the fidelity discipline that governs the rest of the project (every claim re-derived by the test suites) now governs the accessible surface too.

# DeadRamp Base v0.4.0: Phase 4 complete

This release closes Phase 4. The Base now carries the full brand research (600 of 674 vendors researched from citable public identity, 74 held at the neutral federal finish on the record), the build lineage skybridges, the platform layer deck, construction states, the lit interiors, and the experience pass: every room's terminal launches its DeadRamp build, all 101 catalogued live. The fixes in this release came from the owner's playtest of v0.3.15.

## What is new, and why

## What is new, and why

**The Python runtime ships with the site.** Terminals previously loaded their Python runtime from an outside server at first launch; when that load stalled or failed on a visitor's connection, a live room silently fell back to its recorded surface, which reads as placeholder output. The runtime (Pyodide 0.26.4, 13.8 MB) is now vendored into the site itself and loads lazily from the same origin at first launch. World boot is unchanged (plus 1,690 bytes, no runtime bytes). The launch suite now proves a live session with the outside server blocked entirely: the page never even attempts it.

## README (README.md)

# Operation DeadRamp

Clean-room reference implementations of the services listed in the FedRAMP Marketplace: 781 offerings from 674 vendors, one fork per vendor under a single collective repository, with merges governed by the NIST SP 800-218 secure software development framework. Of the 781 offerings, 779 are implemented; the remaining two are recorded as unclassified, with the reason stated, rather than rounded into coverage.

## What this is

The FedRAMP Marketplace is a public index of the cloud services and products the United States government is authorized to buy. Vendors charge premium prices behind that compliance gate. DeadRamp takes the map the government already publishes and builds the open version of the territory:

chunks.h: Operation DeadRamp > What this is
chunks.t:
compliance gate. DeadRamp takes the map the government already publishes and builds the open version of the territory:

- **Index.** Every FedRAMP-authorized vendor and product, registered from public marketplace data.
- **Spec.** Each service modeled from its public surface: documentation, public APIs, and the open standards underneath it.
- **Build.** Clean-room open-source equivalents, one fork per vendor, under one collective repo. Incumbent methods are studied and implemented; no proprietary code is copied.
- **Compliance as shared infrastructure.** The control baselines (NIST SP 800-53) and the CMMC practice sets are public. In DeadRamp they are the shared skeleton every fork hangs on, not a per-vendor toll.

## The two axes

Every fork is placed on two axes:

chunks.h: Operation DeadRamp > The two axes
chunks.t:
are the shared skeleton every fork hangs on, not a per-vendor toll.

## The two axes

Every fork is placed on two axes:

1. **Function** — what it does: service category and model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).
2. **Trust tier** — who may rely on it and at what assurance, matched by CMMC level. FedRAMP Low sits at the CMMC Level 1 tier, FedRAMP Moderate at Level 2 (the NIST SP 800-171 substrate), FedRAMP High at Level 3-adjacent. FedRAMP authorizes products and CMMC certifies organizations, so the tier is a matching equivalence for planning, never a claim that a credential transfers.

Forks with the same function and the same tier are siblings: true substitutes. Forks chain into stacks: IaaS under PaaS under SaaS.

## The merge rule

Merges are NIST compliant by construction:

chunks.h: Operation DeadRamp > The merge rule
chunks.t:
Forks chain into stacks: IaaS under PaaS under SaaS.

## The merge rule

Merges are NIST compliant by construction:

- A merge takes the **union** of the parent forks' control baselines, never the intersection. Merging cannot dilute a control.
- The merged fork inherits the **highest** tier of its parents and must satisfy that tier in full.
- Every merge carries **control traceability**: which parent contributed which controls, auditable from the record.
- The merge process follows NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF): provenance, review, and verification before a merge lands.

Compliance only ratchets one direction. Up.

# DeadRamp Base: Plan (draft, Nov 14, 2026)

Status: brainstorm and plan, at Aries's direction. Build sequence: after fif-ears ships. Nothing here is built yet. This file is uncommitted working state in the deadramp repo.

## The idea in one line

DeadRamp stops being only text: the whole marketplace becomes a walkable VR base, generated from the repo's own data, where every vendor is a building and every service is a room you can stand inside.

- `forks.json` registry: 781 offerings, 674 distinct vendors.
- 101 group directories on two axes: function (accounting, ai, cybersecurity, cloud-infrastructure-hosting, collaboration, crm, data-management, development-tools, and the rest) crossed with trust tier (L1, L2, L3, untiered).
- Impact levels: Moderate 450, High 124, Low 24, LI-SaaS 42, Unknown 141.
- Authorization status: FedRAMP Certified 547; pipeline states 234 (Initial Implementation 102, Legacy Ready 53, Agency In Process 46, FedRAMP In Process 33).
- Built state: 779 of 781 offerings built; 2 honestly unclassified (TERIDA CLASsoft, USDA vGov). 40 gap entries re-scoped to the platform layer under PLATFORM-LAYER.md; union merges carry parent lineage.

## Layout law: one spiral, at every scale

Design reference (Aries, Nov 14, 2026): the worlds of Skyrim, Oblivion, and Dragon Age 2, where travel distance is governed by winding paths at every size, so a compact world feels vast. His words: things are a distance of a spiral no matter how close or far, small or large, it is all spirals. The spiral is therefore scale-invariant in the Base, not just the street plan:

- World scale: a single spiral boulevard is the whole map. Districts (the function groups) are placed in order along the spiral; inside a district, vendor buildings line the boulevard in registry order.
- District scale: each district is its own

chunks.h: DeadRamp Base: Plan (draft, Nov 14, 2026) > Layout law: one spiral, at every scale
chunks.t:
inside a district, vendor buildings line the boulevard in registry order.
- District scale: each district is its own 

smaller spiral off the main boulevard, so entering a district feels like descending into its own coil.
- Building scale: inside a tower, floors are reached by a spiral ramp or stair around a central atrium, one offering per turn; a small office is a single coil.
- Room scale: inside a large service room, exhibits and terminals arrange around a spiral path from the door to the service's core exhibit.
- Why it matters mechanically: path length is always much longer than straight-line distance, which is what makes those game worlds feel big, and here it doubles as the streaming budget: you are always turning, so the engine only ever owes you the next arc of the coil, at every scale.
- Wayfinding is the law Aries named: everything is one spiral away. You can always reach any

chunks.h: DeadRamp Base: Plan (draft, Nov 14, 2026) > Layout law: one spiral, at every scale
chunks.t:
the coil, at every scale.
- Wayfinding is the law Aries named: everything is one spiral away. You can always reach any

thing by following the spiral inward or outward; you cannot get lost in a grid.
- The spiral is also the performance trick: sightlines curve, so draw distance stays short and districts stream in and out naturally on weak hardware.
- Placement is deterministic math (parametric spiral, fixed spacing rules), not hand placement: same catalog in, same city out, seed-locked and testable.

## Buildings and rooms

- One building per vendor (674). Height and footprint scale with offering count: a single-offering vendor is a small office; a multi-offering vendor is a tower, one floor band per offering.
- One room per offering (781). The room is the service: its name, tier badge, status, and its real build data on the walls: the service's own controls, its reference implementation

The animation in a room matches what the service does.
- Status is architecture, honestly: Certified offerings are finished, lit buildings. Pipeline offerings are under construction: scaffolding, cranes, exposed frame, in proportion to their status. The 2 unclassified offerings are surveyed empty lots with a plaque saying exactly that. Platform-layer

## Stack (quality over ego, per Aries)

- Rendering: Three.js in the browser, WebXR for VR. One build serves Quest Browser (Quest 2 and newer), phones (touch twin-stick, optional gyro look), and desktop (WASD plus mouse). No app store, no sideload, standards-first like everything else in the portfolio.
- World generation: the Polyglot Procedural Engine supplies the procedural city and building math (it already generates cities with zero asset files). Where PPE has no piece and an open-source library does it better, the library wins: Aries's order is quality, not ego. All generation is procedural from the catalog; zero hand-modeled assets required for v1.
- Data pipeline: a small exporter in this repo emits `base-catalog.json` from `forks.json` plus the group structure (district assignment, spiral coordinates, room archetype, status styling), consumed by the generator.

## Performance budget (Quest 2 is the floor)

- Exteriors: instanced shells, merged geometry per district, one texture atlas.
- Interiors: only the building you are inside is fully built; every other building is a shell. Rooms in a building build on entry, release on exit.
- Targets to verify on device, not assume: stable frame rate in VR on Quest 2 in the densest district, draw calls and memory inside budget, load from URL to standing in the plaza in seconds, not minutes.

## Brand layer and integrity standard (Aries, Nov 14, 2026)

The one-line constitution, in Aries's words: it is our version of each FedRAMP vendor, their products, their services, their office, built by us from the public record.

The Base is built to government contractor standards: it represents the vendors with integrity and is never rushed or sloppy. Two layers govern every building:

standards: it represents the vendors with integrity and is never rushed or sloppy. Two layers govern every building:

- The federal grammar (the constant): one institutional architecture language across the whole Base, order, symmetry, serious materials, security detailing, gravitas. This is what makes 674 vendors read as one federal installation.
- The brand layer (the variable): inside that grammar, each building wears its vendor's own brand identity, starting with color scheme (Aries's example: Meta is blue and white), then finishes and interior character as phases deepen. The building should be recognizable as that vendor before you read the sign.

# Energy Not Enemy: The Working Model

A working simulation of the solar steam generator described in *Energy Not
Enemy* by Aries Hilton. The book argues; this model demonstrates. Sunlight
is gathered by a parabolic-profile Fresnel lens, water becomes steam in a
closed loop, the steam turns a turbine and a generator, and at night the
steam condenses and the water comes home. There are no solar panels in this
machine, and none in this simulation.

The web page shows the plant in three dimensions, part by part, with the
energy measured at every phase while it runs. The city is a user input: the
page fetches real hourly sunlight and temperature for the place you choose
and runs the same machine on that weather.

## Fidelity statement

This is a lumped-parameter model. Real equations, solved live: solar
position, concentration, a two-phase boiler on the saturation curve, steam
properties from hand-coded correlations, a direction-dependent Tesla valve,
a turbine on the enthalpy drop, a dynamic condenser, and a water inventory
ledger. It is not a mesh CFD or finite-element model, it resolves no
component in space, and it is not a measurement of a built machine. Where
the simulation and the book disagree, the disagreement is published in the
claims table below and in `results/claims-check.json`, never smoothed
over.

## README (README.md)

# Frozen In Flames Channel Strip

A recording channel strip implemented with the Web Audio API and running entirely in the browser: a selectable processing chain is applied to a live microphone input or an uploaded audio file, with metering throughout and the processed result recorded as WAV. No dedicated hardware, no server, and no account are required.

## Live demonstration

chunks.t:
processed result recorded as WAV. No dedicated hardware, no server, and no account are required.

## Live demonstration

- [Channel Strip](https://frozen-in-flames.github.io/fif-channel-strip/): the full application, running in the browser.

## Product line, not a one-off

The app is built as a product line. The shell (audio engine start, sources, meters, recorder, WAV export) knows nothing about DSP. Every chain is a **suite** plugged in through a registry (`suites.js`): each suite carries its own name, description, stage list, and patent ledger reference, and appears as a choice on the startup screen. Adding a future suite means registering a new file. The shell is never touched.

The first suite in the registry is **Vocal Nine**, documented below.

## Philosophy

chunks.t:

The first suite in the registry is **Vocal Nine**, documented below.

## Philosophy

Understand the input before treating it. The app opens with diagnosis, then treats problems in signal order: measure the room, silence it, kill the ringing, fix the capsule, shape the tone, control the dynamics, tame the peaks.

## The Vocal Nine chain

Every stage can be bypassed independently. Signal order:

1. **Analyze** - 64-band real-time FFT spectrum, continuous spectrum display, true-peak readout, noise floor readout, clip indicator, DC-offset indicator. Shows what is wrong with the input before any processing touches it.
2. **Noise print** - capture 1.5 seconds of room tone. The app stores the per-band noise profile, draws it over the spectrum, and auto-suggests the expander threshold from it. This is how a noisy room gets measured instead of guessed at.
3. **E

chunks.h: Frozen In Flames Channel Strip > The Vocal Nine chain
chunks.t:
and auto-suggests the expander threshold from it. This is how a noisy room gets measured instead of guessed at.
3. **E

xpander** - downward expander with a smooth logarithmic envelope and adjustable ratio. Quiets the room between phrases instead of chopping them. Threshold auto-suggested from the noise print.
4. **Feedback Killer** - hunts sustained ringing using the Sabine criteria (constant frequency, growing magnitude, no harmonics, persistent across spectra) and suppresses it with narrow automatic notch filters. Room scan finds modal peaks below 300 Hz. Manual notch add and clear included.
5. **Cleanup** - steep high-pass (40-220 Hz) against handling thumps and rumble, plus Q-30 hum notches at 50 or 60 Hz and harmonics.
6. **Mic Fix** - iPhone transducer correction: tames the harsh 3.3 kHz capsule resonance peak and restores 240 Hz chest body. Followed by the 4-band corrective EQ (l

chunks.h: Frozen In Flames Channel Strip > The Vocal Nine chain
chunks.t:
tames the harsh 3.3 kHz capsule resonance peak and restores 240 Hz chest body. Followed by the 4-band corrective EQ (l

ow shelf, two peaking mids with Q, high shelf).
7. **De-esser** - split-band: compresses only the high band above 6.8 kHz, leaves the voice alone.
8. **Exciter** - high-passed sidechain through asymmetric saturation synthesizes 2nd and 3rd harmonics for air and presence.
9. **Dynamics** - compressor (threshold, ratio, attack, release, live gain-reduction meter), tanh saturation for body, and a 1 ms brickwall limiter that tames the harsh transient peaks cheap mics exaggerate.
10. **Studio Cleanup (toggle)** - deep spectral work in one STFT pass: noise reduction from your noise print (Novatel method), late-reverb suppression (Habets/Lebart exponential-decay model), and a dual-envelope transient shaper. ## Presets

- **Clean**: flat EQ, gentle compression, saturation off. A transparent starting point.
- **Vocal Punch**: high-passed lows, presence lift around 3 kHz, firm compression, a touch of drive.
- **Warm Tape**: boosted lows, rolled-off highs, soft compression, heavier saturation.

## How each problem gets solved

- **Noisy room**: the noise print measures the room tone per frequency band, the expander quiets everything below it, the feedback killer removes sustained ringing, and Studio Cleanup subtracts the noise spectrum itself.
- **Cheap mic harshness**: the limiter tames exaggerated transient peaks, Mic Fix corrects the capsule resonance, the de-esser controls sibilance, the exciter restores harmonic life, and the EQ shapes the rest.
- **Room resonances**: the room scanner finds narrow modal peaks below 300 Hz and notches them; hum notches kill mains buzz.
- **Not knowing what is wrong**: the analyzer shows the 64-band spectrum, true peak, noise floor, clipping, and DC offset live, so every treatment decision is based on measured signal.

## Implementation mapping: which method step each build choice came from

- **Feedback detection (Sabine US5245665A).** The patent's detector: FFT successive
  spectra, find the max-magnitude bin, test it against its harmonics/subharmonics
  by a factor (feedback has no harmonics; voice/music does), require persistence
  across N successive spectra, then place a programmable narrow notch.
  Our `finishHunt`: three FFT snapshots 350 ms apart; candidate bin must hold
  level across all three (persistence), must not decay (growing magnitude:
  v2 >= v0 - 1.5 dB), and bins at 2f and 3f must sit at least 12 dB below the
  candidate (harmonic-richness discrimination). Narrow local-maximum contrast
  check mirrors the patent's peak isolation. Placement: Q=12 biquad notches
  (Rauland-Borg US4088835A).

# fif-ears

- Repository: fif-ears
- Description: Deterministic audio analysis for language models: a seven-layer pipeline (signal, rhythm, structure, harmony, transcription, events, expression) translating an audio file into a structured report. Python, NumPy, SciPy; no learned models in the core pipeline; values reported with confidence, including honest nulls.
- URL: https://github.com/Frozen-In-Flames/fif-ears
- Primary language: Python
- Last push: 2026-11-16T19:40:15Z

## README (README.md)

# fif-ears

Deterministic audio analysis for language models and agents.

A language model has no auditory input channel: presented with an
audio file, it receives a filename, not a sound. fif-ears closes that
gap by measurement. It analyses a file with stated algorithms and
translates the result into structured data that any model can reason
over, with every value reported alongside its confidence, including
honest nulls where the evidence does not support a determination.

chunks.h: fif-ears > Live demonstration
chunks.t:
## Live demonstration

- [fif-ears in the browser](https://frozen-in-flames.github.io/fif-ears/): the identical analysis package running under Pyodide; an uploaded file is analysed locally and the full report is produced in the page.

Give it an audio file. It returns two files:

- `report.json`: a structured, layered report (schema in SCHEMA.md).
- `report.md`: the same content as a timed narrative written for an AI
  reader: what sounds, where the beats fall, the estimated key and
  chords, where sections change, what the dynamics and groove are
  doing, and the words, if a transcription engine is installed.

The contract is universal and model-agnostic. No dependency on any
agent framework, vendor, or model family. Any agent that can run a
command or read a file can use it.

## The standard

The standard for this tool is to hear enough to use the data. Any
quality of sound that is not yet translated into a measurement is an
open method: researched next, listed openly at the end of every report
and in this README. Nothing here is declared impossible.

One accuracy rule sits underneath that standard and never moves: a
layer reports its real status and never fabricates output. If a layer
cannot run, its status says so and its fields are null. That is an
accuracy rule, not a hearing limit: the translation is missing, the
hearing is the roadmap.

chunks.h: fif-ears > Install and run
chunks.t:
## Install and run

Requirements: Python 3.10 or later, numpy, scipy, and ffmpeg on the
PATH (used to decode audio formats).

```sh
pip install -e .
ears analyze path/to/audio.m4a --out path/to/report-dir
```

Without installing:

```sh
python -m ears analyze path/to/audio.wav --out path/to/report-dir
```

## Layers

| Layer | What it measures | Status |
|---|---|---|
| signal | duration, sample rate, channels, peak and RMS level, clipping, spectral centroid, bandwidth, rolloff, stereo width | IMPLEMENTED (classical) |
| rhythm | onset times, tempo with confidence and alternative metrical levels, beat grid refined against onsets | IMPLEMENTED (classical) |
| structure | novelty curve and section boundaries, ported from the Frozen In Flames Reactor clip-start analysis | IMPLEMENTED (classical, ported) |
| harmony | YIN pitch track, chroma, key estimate, per-section chord with margin-based confidence | IMPLEMENTED (classical) |
| words | speech transcription | IMPLEMENTED when a local Whisper engine is installed (optional dependency: openai-whisper or faster-whisper); otherwise reports status `not_installed` |
| events | sound segments labeled speech-like, music-like, noise-like, silence, from classical feature rules | IMPLEMENTED (classical reference); trained-model adapter is INTERFACE ONLY |
| expression | dynamics contour and slopes, groove and microtiming against the grid, swing, timbre proxies (brightness, warmth, roughness), harmonic tension curve | IMPLEMENTED (classical) |

chunks.h: fif-ears > What the numbers mean, briefly
chunks.t:
## What the numbers mean, briefly

- Chord confidence is a margin: how far the best chord template beats
  the runner-up. Flat, ambiguous input (noise) scores near zero and
  reports no chord, instead of a confident wrong answer.
- Tempo is chosen from autocorrelation peaks scored with a standard
  log-Gaussian prior centered at 120 BPM. The report lists the other
  metrical levels measured, so a reader can see the choice that was
  made. The beat grid is then refit against detected onsets.
- Groove is measured in milliseconds against the fitted grid: mean and
  spread of attack deviations, and the mean delay of offbeat onsets
  (the swing number). Positive means behind the grid.
- Harmonic tension runs 0 to 1 per section: circle-of-fifths distance
  of the section chord from the tonic, blended with the chord template
  residual. A clean tonic chord reads near 0.
- Silence is the standing negative control: silence in, nothing out.
  No beats, no notes, no chords, no events beyond silence, flat
  dynamics. The test suite asserts this on every run.

chunks.h: fif-ears > Tests and verification
chunks.t:
## Tests and verification

Tests are synthesized fixtures with known answers, asserted as
numbers, plus negative and mutation controls (silence, white noise, a
120 BPM fixture that must fail the 130 BPM hypothesis, a reversed
crescendo that must flip its measured slope sign).

```sh
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Verified at build time (this machine, Python 3.12, numpy 1.26,
scipy 1.11):

- Test suite: 15 of 15 passing in about 4 seconds.

- End-to-end on a real 91.7 second M4A (a performed track whose
  filename states 155 BPM, A Phrygian dominant): fif-ears measured
  151.74 BPM (the 152 BPM metrical level chosen over a stronger slow
  pulse at 44.36 BPM, both listed in the report), dominant pitch D3,
  key estimate D minor at 0.866 correlation, 8 sections with the first
  internal boundary at 2.66 seconds (the same first boundary the
  Reactor analysis finds on this file), 88.4 of 91.7 seconds labeled
  music-like, words layer `not_installed` (no local Whisper on this
  machine).

chunks.h: fif-ears > Tests and verification
chunks.t:
- Honest gaps in that run: the Krumhansl-Schmuckler key vocabulary
  covers major and minor only. A Phrygian dominant is the fifth mode
  of D harmonic minor, so D minor is the closest answer in that
  vocabulary. Modal key vocabularies are an open method (below).

chunks.h: fif-ears > Open methods
chunks.t:
## Open methods

Translations not yet built, in the order they are being researched:

- Modal and extended key vocabularies (Phrygian dominant, harmonic and
  melodic minor modes, borrowed harmony) beyond major/minor profiles.
- Trained sound-event classification: the events layer defines the
  adapter interface (YAMNet or PANNs style) so a trained model can be
  fused with the classical reference without changing the schema.
- Polyphonic note transcription: an adapter point for models in the
  Basic Pitch family (an ONNX model is already vendored in the Frozen
  In Flames beatbox-to-midi repo) behind the same honesty rules.
- Emotion and felt-quality naming: the expression layer measures the
  correlates (dynamics, groove, timbre, tension). Naming feelings from
  correlates is a translation still being researched.
- Speaker separation and identification for multi-voice recordings.

## Evaluation datasets

Free academic datasets suitable for calibrating each layer are
documented in [eval/README.md](eval/README.md) (LibriSpeech for words,
FSD50K for events, MUSDB18 for music separation and structure, MAESTRO
for piano pitch). They are documented as pointers only: fif-ears
downloads nothing and bundles no third-party data.

## Reuse notes

Built by porting proven Frozen In Flames code rather than reinventing
it: the structure layer is a Python port of Reactor's section-start
analysis, and the pitch layer ports the YIN approach from
midi-vocal-trainer. The rest is new, small, and deterministic:
numpy and scipy only, no randomness, no network, no downloads at
runtime.

chunks.h: Vendored package note > What this is
chunks.t:
## What this is

fif-ears gives agents ears. Most AI models cannot hear: hand a model an audio file and it gets a filename, not a sound. This tool listens as measurement and translates what is in the audio into structured data any model can reason over. It was built open, for every agent and model that shares this limit, not for one product or one model family. The contract is universal: an audio file goes in through the CLI, and two files come out, report.json (layered, schema documented in SCHEMA.md) and report.md (the same content as a timed narrative written for an AI reader).

## Why

Aries Hilton's standing rule is that a limit is an unassigned method, not a fact. Hearing decomposes into methods: rhythm, pitch, harmony, structure, words, events, and expression all have math. This release assigns those methods and proves each one against ground truth, so agents stop guessing about audio from filenames and waveforms.

chunks.h: Vendored package note > The seven layers
chunks.t:
## The seven layers

- signal: duration, levels, clipping, spectral summary, stereo width. Implemented, tested.
- rhythm: onsets, tempo with auditable metrical levels, beat grid. Implemented, tested.
- structure: section boundaries, a faithful port of the novelty analysis from Reactor. Implemented, tested.
- harmony: pitch track (YIN), key estimate, per-segment chords with margin confidence, honest nulls where the evidence is weak. Implemented, tested.
- words: transcription when a local Whisper engine is installed (openai-whisper or faster-whisper). On a machine without one the layer reports not_installed and a null transcript. It never fabricates words.
- events: non-music sound segmentation (silence, speech-like, music-like, noise-like) as a classical reference implementation. The trained-model adapter is an interface only, labeled as such in code.
- expression: the feel, translated. Dynamics contour and per-section slopes, groove (beat deviation and swing in milliseconds), timbre proxies (brightness, warmth, roughness), and a harmonic tension curve built only from chords the harmony layer actually reported.

# frozen-in-flames-deblur

- Repository: frozen-in-flames-deblur
- Description: Classical image deblurring without learned models: inversion of motion, defocus, and Gaussian blur, with low-resolution upscaling. Point-spread functions are estimated by an automated sweep scored by spectral null fingerprinting. Verified by 41 passing tests.
- URL: https://github.com/Frozen-In-Flames/frozen-in-flames-deblur
- Primary language: Python

## README (README.md)

# Frozen In Flames Deblur

Classical image deblurring and enhancement. **No AI, no machine learning,
no trained models** — just signal processing: deconvolution with
point-spread functions that are identified from the image's own spectrum,
plus unsharp masking, CLAHE, and high-quality upscaling. Built on OpenCV,
scikit-image, and numpy.

scikit-image, and numpy.

It removes the three common single-image blurs, handles low
resolution, treats noise-dominated photos without pretending they are
blurred, and can restore foreground and background separately when
the blur changes across one photo. Parameters are zoom-aware (a
photo taken at a digital zoom reports its blur in sensor terms), a
recorded-video mode deblurs whole clips frame by frame, and a live
clarify view serves camera glasses and phone cameras as an
accessibility aid (see "Camera glasses" below):

| `focus` | Out of focus (defocus) | Disk PSF sweep (radius), deconvolution |
| `gaussian` | General lens softnes

never leaves your device.

Two staging choices exist only because browser math is slow, and both

## How the blur is identified

Deconvolution only works when the PSF matches the real blur, so the sweep
scores every candidate **spectrally** — it never trusts how a restoration
"looks" to a sharpness metric. Two preparation steps come first, because
both were measured failure modes:

"looks" to a sharpness metric. Two preparation steps come first, because
both were measured failure modes:

* **Estimation reads a denoised copy.** Noise is measured on the
  untouched input (Immerkaer's estimator, averaged over the flattest
  half of the image so texture cannot inflate it), then the sweep runs
  on a copy denoised at a strength scaled to that measurement.
  Restoration still works on the original pixels. Heavy sensor noise
  otherwise buries the fingerprint entirely.
* **Scoring reads the detail layer.** The scorer sees the estimation
  image minus its sigma-2 gaussian blur. Flat regions and smooth
  gradients have no detail layer, so only edge-rich regions vote, and
  the low frequencies where content-layout fringes live are removed
  while the band carrying the blur fingerprint is kept. (A spatially
  multiplied edge mask was tried for this and measured to

  read — the mask's own spectrum convolves into the fingerprint band.
  The edge mask itself is used where it is sound: segmented mode.)

Then every candidate is scored on:

* **Null fingerprint.** A blur kernel's transfer function has nulls:
  motion blur carves parallel null stripes into the spectrum, a defocus
  disk carves rings, a gaussian carves none. The candidate's null map is
  cosine-matched against the observed image's null map, minus a chance
  baseline (the same match with the candidate's map displaced), so dense
  kernels can't win by overlapping everything a little.
* **Radial profile residual.** After removing the candidate's radial
  log-spectrum from the observed one, what remains should be a straight
  line (natural spectra are roughly po

  non-line remainder measures how wrong the candidate's strength is.
* **The auto decision.** Motion is chosen only if its winner passes
  three guards: its null match clears a floor (0.10); its match is
  *specific* — it beats the longest sweepable kernel (31 px) at the
  same angle by at least 0.05, because chance correlation grows with
  kernel length and piles up at the longest length with no interior
  peak, while a true kernel's match peaks at its own length and falls;
  and the isotropic evidence stays below its cap, so a strong
  focus/gaussian explanation is not overridden by a coincidental
  directional match. The isotropic winner is accepted when it reduces
  the radial residual by at least 0.05 versus a near-identity kernel.

Sharpness-of-restoration scoring was tried first and measured to fail:
a wrong-PSF deconvolution manufactures ghost edges that sharpness metrics
reward, and any "how close is the reblur" measure is gamed by timid
kernels that barely change the image. Details and numbers: TEST-REPORT.md.

## Segmented mode: foreground and background, deblurred both

The design, in the owner's words: "there should be some sort of edge
mask that you use to sort background from foreground to deblur both."
The algorithm is classical throughout:

1. **Tile and classify.** The estimation luminance is tiled (about
   160 px tiles, fewer on small images). Each tile is classified by
   spectral scoring over the coarse candidate grids, on its detail
   layer. Tiles whose mean edge density is too low to carry evidence
   are marked weak and do not vote.
2. **Region growing.** Confident tiles join 4-neighbours whose
   parameters are similar (same family; motion within 15 degrees and
   6 px; focus within 2 px; gaussian within 1.2 sigma). Connected
   components are the candidate regions; the two largest win. Every

## Camera glasses: zoom, recorded video, and the live view

The toolkit's glasses architecture (full note: `docs/glasses.md`)
is the split the open camera-glasses class is built on: the glasses
are the camera, the paired device does the processing, and there
are two modes at two honestly labeled speeds.

chunks.h: is wiener, the fast method, and there is no upscale. > Camera glasses: zoom, recorded video, and the live view
chunks.t:
glasses
are the camera, the paired device does the processing, and there
are two modes at two honestly labeled speeds.

**Zoom.** Digital zoom crops the sensor image and enlarges the
crop, so a sensor blur of B px spans z*B px in the view at zoom z.
With `--zoom z` (or `Settings.zoom`), estimates are still measured
on the image as given (view space), but the report converts them to
**sensor space** (view / z), and manual pins are read as sensor
space and restored with the view-space kernel pin × z. Angles never
scale. On a swept run the zoom changes no pixels, only what the
numbers mean; on a pinned run it is what makes the pin the same
physical blur at any zoom. Without it, a 2x-zoomed photo's blur
reads about twice the sensor truth, which is exactly the miss the
zoom factor exists to remove.

per-frame price). Frames are written at native size; segmented is

## Pipeline order, and why

0. **Measure the noise** on the untouched input (Immerkaer). The
   number drives the estimation denoise strength, the restoration
   denoise strength, and the auto noise decision.
1. **Denoise** — noise is deconvolution's enemy. The restoration base
   gets a fastNlMeans pass whose strength scales with the measured
   noise (h=3 on clean images, the long-standing light pass, ramping
   to h=10 at heavy noise); the separate estimation copy is denoised
   by the sam

2. **Deconvolve at native resolution, luminance only** — the PSF is only
   known at native scale, and blur is linear, so it is undone on a linear
   luminance channel (not LAB L\*, whose nonlinear remap biases the
   recovered parameters). Color follows by the luminance ratio, which
   preserves hue and avoids color fringing. Reflect padding prevents
   border ringing. Methods: Wiener, Richardson-Lucy, or RL with TV
   denoising between chunks (default; suppresses RL's ringing).

## Honest expectations

* Mild to moderate, roughly uniform blur (slight defocus, small camera
  shake, soft lens): this works well.
* Classical processing sharpens and clarifies what is in the image. It
  **cannot invent real detail that heavy blur destroyed**.
* Blur that varies across the image is what `segmented` is for, within
  its limits: two regions maximum, boundaries reso

# Deblur for camera glasses: the architecture

v0.4.0 extends the toolkit from stills to open-source AR glasses
with cameras. This note states the architecture the code implements,
so the claims in the README and on the pages can be checked against
it.

## The split: glasses are the camera, the companion does the work

Open-source camera glasses are built thin: a camera, a small
processor, a radio. The heavy compute lives on the paired device
(phone or computer) the glasses already talk to. This toolkit
follows that shape exactly:

chunks.h: Deblur for camera glasses: the architecture > The split: glasses are the camera, the companion does the work
chunks.t:
lives on the paired device
(phone or computer) the glasses already talk to. This toolkit
follows that shape exactly:

* **Capture on the glasses.** The camera (the glasses', or a phone
  camera standing in for any camera a browser can open) produces
  stills, clips, and the live feed.
* **Processing on the companion.** Everything in this repository
  runs on the companion device, on-device from the user's point of
  view: no server, no upload, in the browser or from the command
  line.

## Two modes, two speeds, honestly labeled

The full engine (the Python package) identifies an unknown blur
from the image's own spectrum and inverts it. That costs seconds
per frame. A live view needs an answer per frame. Pretending one
chain is the other would be a lie in both directions, so there are
two, and each is labeled as what it is:

   full engine. For video (`deblur/video.py`,

   frames, temporally smoothed into a track (median filter within
   family runs, interpolation between samples, family changes step

   parameters using the fast method by default. The run reports its

## The zoom model

Camera glasses zoom by cropping the sensor image and enlarging the
crop (digital zoom). A blur that spans B px on the sensor therefore
spans z*B px in the zoomed view at zoom z, and any measurement made
on the view file is in view pixels. `Settings.zoom` (CLI `--zoom`)
encodes exactly that:

chunks.h: Deblur for camera glasses: the architecture > The zoom model
chunks.t:
z, and any measurement made
on the view file is in view pixels. `Settings.zoom` (CLI `--zoom`)
encodes exactly that:

* estimates are measured in **view space** (the pixels handed in);
* reports and region parameters are stated in **sensor space**
  (view / zoom), so a reading means the same physical blur at any
  zoom level;
* manual pins are stated in **sensor space** and restored with the
  view-space kernel pin x zoom;
* restoration always deconvolves the handed-in image with the
  view-space kernel, so on a swept run zoom relabels the report and
  changes no pixels (the suite asserts the outputs are identical),
  while on a pinned run it is what makes the pin correct;
* angles never scale. Noise is measured on the view as given (zoom
  magnifies grain along with everything else; the number is a view
  measurement and the notes say so).

chunks.h: Deblur for camera glasses: the architecture > The zoom model
chunks.t:
as given (zoom
  magnifies grain along with everything else; the number is a view
  measurement and the notes say so).

The live page applies the same model in miniature: its sharpening
strength auto-scales with the zoom slider
(`clarityForZoom`: x(1 + 0.4(z-1)), capped at 2.2x), because zoom
magnifies blur and noise together.

One measured boundary of the model: the stills estimator's proven
envelope is kernels up to about 21 px in the space it measures.
A 2x zoom of a 15 px sensor blur is a 30 px view kernel, outside
that envelope: the conversion still applies exactly (the suite
asserts it), but the underlying auto read can under-read or decline
at that size, at any zoom. The numbers are in TEST-REPORT.md.

## The named next step: measure the blur at its source

Everything above estimates blur from pixels. Glasses carry
gyroscopes, and the dominant live-view blur is the wearer's own
head motion during each exposure. That blur does not need to be
estimated from the image at all: angular velocity x exposure time
gives the smear's direction and length directly, per frame, from
the IMU. The natural evolution of both modes is IMU-aided PSF:
the live de-smear keyed to the gyro instead of (or checked against)
the phase-correlation readout, and the recorded-video track seeded
from the clip's motion metadata where the glasses provide it. The
pixel estimator remains the fallback for content with no motion
data, and the arbiter when the two disagree.
