# Frozen In Flames: Kindling

## Open Music Creation System

Kindling is an open, professional-grade system that generates, edits, and re-renders complete songs from a persistent scene, reusable creative assets, and an explainable artist profile.

## Live demonstration

chunks.h: Frozen In Flames: Kindling > Live demonstration
chunks.t:
songs from a persistent scene, reusable creative assets, and an explainable artist profile.

## Live demonstration

- [Kindling](https://frozen-in-flames.github.io/frozen-in-flames-kindling/): the system's web implementation, running in the browser.

The name says what it is. Reusable voice characters, virtual instruments, and production presets are the kindling: the prepared fuel you lay down before every song. The musical scene is how you lay the fire. Rendering is the burn. And any song can be rekindled, changed exactly where you want, and burned again.

### What it is

A music-creation system in which a song is a structured, editable *scene* and audio is one rendering of that scene. Three persistent layers sit on top of a generation engine:

chunks.h: Frozen In Flames: Kindling > Live demonstration > What it is
chunks.t:
editable *scene* and audio is one rendering of that scene. Three persistent layers sit on top of a generation engine:

1. The **Musical Scene**: the source of truth for structure, harmony, melody, lyrics, parts, automation, and production.
2. **Creative assets**: saved voice characters, virtual instruments, and production presets, captured once and reused.
3. The **Artist Profile**: an explainable, editable model built from a creator's uploads that supplies context to every tool.

The core loop is **analyze → construct scene → render → inspect → revise**. A user can start from a text prompt, lyrics, a hummed melody, a stem, or a finished recording, and always end up with something they can change locally and re-render.

### Thesis

chunks.h: Frozen In Flames: Kindling > Live demonstration > Thesis
chunks.t:
a stem, or a finished recording, and always end up with something they can change locally and re-render.

### Thesis

Do not compete on one-click song quality. Build an open, inspectable system that turns musical intent into a structured scene, renders it convincingly with reusable voices, instruments, and production styles, learns an explainable picture of each artist, and lets a creator change exactly what they want and nothing else.

### First audience (v1)

Songwriters and producers who want to prototype full songs with vocals, then refine specific parts.

### Quality targets

Every dimension has a numeric threshold, set before training anything, published, and reviewed quarterly. Thresholds live in [targets.yaml](targets.yaml); `tools/check_targets.py` reports which are still unset.

### Hardware tiers

chunks.h: Frozen In Flames: Kindling > Live demonstration > Hardware tiers
chunks.t:
live in [targets.yaml](targets.yaml); `tools/check_targets.py` reports which are still unset.

### Hardware tiers

- **Draft**: single consumer GPU. Fast previews, smaller models.
- **Studio**: workstation GPU. Full-quality local rendering.
- **Hosted**: largest models, batch and long renders.

Every feature states which tiers it supports.

### v1 non-goals

Live-performance accompaniment. Every language on day one. Mobile-native inference. Replacing the DAW (Kindling integrates with existing DAWs through export and plugins instead).

### Build versions

One version per part of the build manual. V1 is Part 1, Product definition (this document). V2 is Part 2, Architecture, and so on through V23, the release checklist. See [VERSIONS.md](VERSIONS.md). Nothing is skipped.

### Spec

### Spec

The full build manual is the spec: [docs/BUILD_MANUAL.md](docs/BUILD_MANUAL.md). Every part has Purpose, Requirements (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), and Acceptance tests. Part 22 gives the build sequence with exit criteria. Part 23 is the release checklist.

### Functional milestone A (V24)

The upload / save / use loop is live in Python. See
[docs/functional-milestone-a.md](docs/functional-milestone-a.md).

```

    --consent-subject "Aries Hilton"

# Architecture (Part 2)

The architecture is data, not prose. `kindling/architecture.py` holds the
seven principles (2.1), the seven layers and 34 components of the component
map (2.2), and the seven data flow stages (2.3). `kindling/interfaces.py`
holds one abstract base class per component: the documented contract.

## Principles

1. The scene is the source of truth.
2. Everything is inspectable and editable.
3. Locality over reroll.
4. Uncertainty is shown.
5. Identity is separate from performance.
6. Open and modular.
7. Consent and provenance are built in.

## Layers

chunks.h: Architecture (Part 2) > Layers
chunks.t:
Identity is separate from performance.
6. Open and modular.
7. Consent and provenance are built in.

## Layers

Interface, workflow, intelligence, assets, generation, production, foundation.
Every component declares which hardware tiers (draft, studio, hosted) it
supports, per Part 1.4.

## Replacing a component

Because the map is data and the contracts are ABCs, any component can be
swapped for another implementation honoring the same interface:

```python
from kindling.architecture import REGISTRY, ComponentSpec

REGISTRY.register(ComponentSpec(
    name="Mixer",
    layer="production",
    interface="kindling.interfaces.Mixer",  # contract must not change
    tiers=["draft", "studio", "hosted"],
    description="My mixer",
    implementation="my_package.MyMixer",
))
```

chunks.h: Architecture (Part 2) > Replacing a component
chunks.t:
tiers=["draft", "studio", "hosted"],
    description="My mixer",
    implementation="my_package.MyMixer",
))
```

The registry refuses a replacement that changes the interface path, so the
contract stays fixed while implementations come and go.

## Data flow

Input arrives (prompt, lyrics, MIDI, stems, or finished audio). The analyzer
and interpreter produce a draft scene with confidences. The user and planner
refine it. The orchestrator renders parts using assets and presets. The mixer
assembles the audio. The user inspects, edits the scene or a region, and
re-renders only what changed. Every step is saved as a version.

## Status

chunks.h: Architecture (Part 2) > Status
chunks.t:
inspects, edits the scene or a region, and
re-renders only what changed. Every step is saved as a version.

## Status

V2 ships the registry, the principles, the data flow, and the 34 interface
contracts. Implementations land one part at a time from V3 onward. Where the
manual requires trained models that do not exist yet, each version ships the
real interface, the evaluation harness, the extension points, and a
deterministic reference implementation, and documents which is which.

# Artist Profile (Part 11)

A persistent, explainable model built from a creator's uploads that
supplies context to every tool.

## Structure (11.1)

chunks.h: Artist Profile (Part 11) > Structure (11.1)
chunks.t:
persistent, explainable model built from a creator's uploads that
supplies context to every tool.

## Structure (11.1)

Five separate, inspectable dimensions: musical_identity,
sound_arrangement, performance, production, variation. Each stores
tendencies (mean/min/max or mode/share) and ranges with observation
counts, plus the evidence behind every observation. Never collapsed
into a single style vector.

## Relationship graph (11.2)

`ProfileGraph` links tracks, sections, and traits. Every edge carries
audible evidence (section, role, pattern). Answers: shared traits
between two tracks (with per-track evidence), outlier traits, and
which traits recur in choruses but not verses.

## Modes (11.3)

chunks.h: Artist Profile (Part 11) > Modes (11.3)
chunks.t:
tracks (with per-track evidence), outlier traits, and
which traits recur in choruses but not verses.

## Modes (11.3)

`detect_modes` splits tracks into separate contexts (sparse vs dense)
when a trait is bimodal. Modes are never blended into an average. New
projects choose: follow a mode, combine modes, or explore.

## Explanations (11.4)

`explain_suggestion` renders a suggestion with its rationale and cites
the uploads and sections it draws on.

## Corrections (11.5)

`apply_correction`: mark a trait track-specific, drop a trait, or keep
only chosen traits. Each correction is versioned in the profile history
and scoped to one dimension; other dimensions are untouched.
`rollback` records the rollback point in the history.

## Scope selection (11.6)

chunks.h: Artist Profile (Part 11) > Scope selection (11.6)
chunks.t:
other dimensions are untouched.
`rollback` records the rollback point in the history.

## Scope selection (11.6)

`select_scope`: full_catalog, chosen_references, era_or_mode, or none.
The resolved scope always names itself; the default is shown, never
hidden.

## Privacy (11.8)

`PrivacyRecord`: private by default, encrypted, owner-exportable,
deletable with cascading removal of derived data (`remove_track`
deletes the track and all its trait observations). Profile data never
enters shared training without a separate explicit opt-in; the flag
defaults to False and is revocable.

## Where it is used (11.7)

Composition, voice characters, virtual instruments, presets,
arrangement assistance, and editing all take a scope and read the
relevant dimensions. The profile supplies context; it never dictates.

## Part 2. Architecture

**2.1 Principles.**

1. **The scene is the source of truth.** Rendered audio is derived and can always be regenerated from the scene, assets, seeds, and settings.
2. **Everything is inspectable and editable.** No hidden intermediates the user cannot see or change.
3. **Locality over reroll.** A targeted edit changes the target.
4. **Uncertainty is shown.** Inferred things carry confidence and alternatives. Insufficient input produces a warning, not a quiet guess.
5. **Identity is separate from performance.** A voice or instrument stays itself while its performance changes.
6. **Open and modular.** Each component has a documented interface and can be replaced.
7. **Consent and provenance are built in**, not bolted on (Part 19).

| Intelligence | Prompt interpreter, composition planner, arrangement assistant, profile engine, reference analyzer |
| Assets | Voice characters, virtual instruments, production presets |
| Generation | Audio codec and latent space, song renderer, vocal renderer, instrument renderer, editing models |

2. The analyzer and interpreter produce a *draft scene* with confidences.
3. The user and planner refine it.
4. The orchestrator renders parts using assets and presets.
5. The mixer assembles the audio.
6. The user inspects, edits the scene or a region, and re-renders only what changed.
7. Every step is saved as a version.

## Part 3. The Musical Scene

**Purpose.** One shared representation connecting intent, symbolic music, performance, and audio.

**3.1 Contents.** The scene MUST represent:

- **Timeline:** tempo map, meter map, key map, section boundaries in bars and seconds.
- **Sections:** type (intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, outro, custom), length, energy target, density target.
- **Harmo

- **Melody:** note events with timing and pitch, or contour-only form.
- **Lyrics:** text, language, syllable segmentation, syllable-to-note alignment, phrasing marks.
- **Parts:** one per musical role, with assigned instrument asset, note and articulation data, dynamics, and expression curves.
- **Vocal parts:** assigned voice character, performance instruction, lyric lines.
- **Automation:** lanes for any parameter, per section or continuous.
- **Production graph:** preset reference or inline chain, routing, sends and returns.
- **Render settings:** sample rate, seeds, model and asset versions, quality tier.
- **Provenance:** who or what created each element.

**3.2 Per-element metadata.** Every element carries `source` (user, planner, inferred, imported), `confidence`, `locked` (the system must not change it), and `realization` level.

**3.3 Realization levels.** The system MUST work with partially realized scenes. An element can exist at four levels:

1. *Intent*: described in words or tags (for example, "bigger second chorus").
2. *Symbolic*: notes, chords, and lyrics with timing.
3. *Performance*: expressive timing, dynamics, articulations, vocal delivery parameters.
4. *Audio*: a rendered take, linked to the exact scene version and seeds that produced it.

**3.5 Operations.** The scene store MUST support immutable versions, branches, element-level diffs, merges with conflict reporting, and content-addressed references to assets. A diff MUST be readable by a person (for example, "chorus 2 energy 0.6 → 0.8; added pad part").

**3.6 Import and export.** Import MIDI, MusicXML, stems, and finished audio (through analysis, with confidences). Export MIDI, stems, mixed audio, and the scene itself in an open, documented format.

**Acceptance tests.** Round-trip a MIDI file through the scene and back with no note loss. Re-render a saved scene on the same tier and pass the reproducibility test. Edit one section and confirm the diff lists only that section's elements.

## Part 4. Data pipeline

**Purpose.** Reproducible, traceable data with labels good enough to train structured, editable models.

**4.1 Stages.** Ingest and validate; normalize format and apply the loudness policy; deduplicate; segment; analyze (tempo, beats, key, chords, sections, energy); detect and separate vocals and instruments while keeping the original mix; transcribe lyrics and align words and syllables to the singing; label instruments and roles; score annotation quality; assign splits; write the record.

**4.2 Per-track record.** Each record MUST store: content hash; source and acquisition method; license or consent status and its terms; allowed uses (train, evaluate, none); processing versions; every derived label with a confidence; split assignment; and a deletion handle.

**4.3 Rules.**

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 4. Data pipeline
chunks.t:
processing versions; every derived label with a confidence; split assignment; and a deletion handle.

**4.3 Rules.**

- **Splits are fixed early and never leak.** Deduplicate across splits, including near-duplicates and alternate mixes of the same song.
- **Provenance is queryable.** You must be able to answer "which training items came from this source" and filter by license status.
- **Deletion propagates.** Removing an item or a user upload MUST exclude it from future training runs and remove dependent derived assets where policy requires.
- **Low-confidence labels are marked, not hidden.** Training code can threshold them.

**4.4 Data browser.** Build an internal tool to search by any label, play audio with aligned lyrics and section markers, inspect label confidence, and flag failures. Researchers should use it weekly. If nobody opens it, the pipeline is not trusted.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 4. Data pipeline
chunks.t:
label confidence, and flag failures. Researchers should use it weekly. If nobody opens it, the pipeline is not trusted.

**4.5 Policy workstream.** Rights and licensing policy depends on jurisdiction, sources, and distribution. Assign an owner, write the policy before the first large training run, and encode its outcome in the license fields above.

**Acceptance tests.** Pick 100 random records: each is traceable to source, license status, and processing versions. Pick 100 aligned lyrics: median word alignment error meets the Part 1 target. A leakage audit finds zero cross-split duplicates.

## Part 5. Audio representation

**Purpose.** A compressed representation that can be generated efficiently without losing what musicians care about.

**Requirements.**

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 5. Audio representation
chunks.t:
representation that can be generated efficiently without losing what musicians care about.

**Requirements.**

- MUST preserve timbre, transients, stereo image, and fine musical detail at the target sample rate (44.1 or 48 kHz stereo).
- MUST support decoding isolated regions, because editing needs local reconstruction.
- SHOULD support stem-aware or multi-track latents so separate parts can be generated and replaced.
- SHOULD offer more than one compression rate: a fast draft rate and a high-fidelity rate.
- MUST be evaluated on its own before any generator is built on it.

**Acceptance tests.** Reconstruction listening tests on drums, vocals, solo piano, dense mixes, and quiet material. Objective checks for spectral error, transient smearing, stereo correlation, and loudness drift. Encode-edit-decode round trips that show no seams at region boundaries.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 6. Song planning and rendering
chunks.t:
stereo correlation, and loudness drift. Encode-edit-decode round trips that show no seams at region boundaries.

## Part 6. Song planning and rendering

**6.1 Prompt interpreter.** Converts natural language, tags, lyrics, and controls into a draft scene. It MUST output a scene the user can read and MUST list its assumptions (for example, "assumed 4/4, 92 BPM, F# minor").

**6.2 Composition planner.** Proposes form, harmony, motifs, energy curve, and arrangement, conditioned on the scene, assets, and any selected profile context. It MUST offer alternatives on request and respect locked elements.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 6. Song planning and rendering
chunks.t:
the scene, assets, and any selected profile context. It MUST offer alternatives on request and respect locked elements.

**6.3 Renderer.** Converts scene, assets, and preset into audio. Run a structured bake-off between autoregressive token models, parallel latent-generation models, and a planner-plus-renderer hybrid. Judge them against the Part 1 targets, not demos. Keep the renderer behind a stable interface (scene fragment in; audio and metadata out) so the winner can be replaced later.

**6.4 Hierarchical generation.** Plan at song level, refine at section level, render at phrase or chunk level. Chunks MUST overlap, and each chunk MUST be conditioned on the surrounding audio and scene context, before and after it where available.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 6. Song planning and rendering
chunks.t:
and each chunk MUST be conditioned on the surrounding audio and scene context, before and after it where available.

**6.5 Long-form coherence.** Implement and test: tempo and harmony consistency across boundaries; motif return and development; energy curves across the whole song; intentional transitions (fills, risers, breaks) instead of fades; consistent vocal identity; no skipped or repeated lyric lines.

**6.6 Preview tiers.** Provide a *sketch* (seconds, lowest cost), a *draft* (good enough for decisions), and a *final* (full quality). A change heard in the sketch SHOULD predict the change in the final.

**Acceptance tests.** On the fixed suite (Part 17), raters score transitions and coherence above threshold; automatic checks show tempo drift and key violations below threshold; lyric completeness is met on every test song.

drift and key violations below threshold; lyric completeness is met on every test song.

## Part 7. Vocals and lyrics

**Purpose.** Vocals are the hardest quality challenge. Treat them as their own system.

**Requirements.**

- MUST align lyrics to melody at syllable level, with per-language pronunciation handling (grapheme-to-phoneme, stress, elision).
- MUST support line-level regeneration: change a line, realign it, and re-sing only that line while neighboring lines keep their audio.
- MUST expose expressive controls: dynamics, breathiness, vibrato, belt, whisper, phrasing, push or lay-back timing, doubles, and harmonies.
- MUST report intelligibility automatically (ASR on isolated rendered vocals) and flag lines below threshold.
- SHOULD support multilingual lyrics and code-switching. List supported languages explicitly and test each separately.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 7. Vocals and lyrics
chunks.t:
SHOULD support multilingual lyrics and code-switching. List supported languages explicitly and test each separately.

**Acceptance tests.** Word error rate on rendered vocals below the Part 1 threshold for each declared language. A changed lyric line re-renders with unchanged surrounding audio (Part 12 locality). Blinded vocal-quality ratings by trained vocalists.

## Part 8. Voice characters

**Purpose.** A saved, reusable singing identity that can perform new lyrics and melodies.

**8.1 Asset specification.** A voice character MUST contain:

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 8. Voice characters
chunks.t:
identity that can perform new lyrics and melodies.

**8.1 Asset specification.** A voice character MUST contain:

- Identity representation: what makes the voice this voice.
- Usable range map, with reliability per register.
- Timbral traits and register transitions.
- Pronunciation and language behavior.
- Expressive controls and their valid ranges.
- Reference summary: what material it was built from and how sufficient that material was.
- Version, owner, consent record, and creation provenance.

**8.2 Identity versus performance.** The performance instruction (soft, belt, whisper, bright, laid-back) is a separate input. Changing it MUST NOT change identity. Test this directly.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 8. Voice characters
chunks.t:
(soft, belt, whisper, bright, laid-back) is a separate input. Changing it MUST NOT change identity. Test this directly.

**8.3 Building from a reference.** Accept short and noisy references. Run a **sufficiency report** before building: coverage of pitch range, vowels, dynamics, and registers. When a requested performance is outside what the reference supports (for example, a high belt from a reference of soft mid-range singing), the system MUST say so and offer options instead of producing an unstable imitation.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 8. Voice characters
chunks.t:
of soft mid-range singing), the system MUST say so and offer options instead of producing an unstable imitation.

**8.4 Consent and control.** Creating a voice character from a person's voice MUST require a recorded consent statement tied to that person and verified against the reference audio, or documented rights for a licensed or synthetic source. Store ownership. Let the owner revoke and delete. Mark rendered vocals with a robust, detectable watermark and provenance metadata. This is a release requirement, not a later feature.

**8.5 Reuse.** Save, version, share (with permissions), and fork characters. Every render records which version was used.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 8. Voice characters
chunks.t:
Reuse.** Save, version, share (with permissions), and fork characters. Every render records which version was used.

**Acceptance tests.** Identity similarity holds across new lyrics, melodies, registers, and styles above threshold. Listeners do not judge two performance styles of one character to be different people. The sufficiency report correctly flags deliberately inadequate references. A revoked character cannot be used for new renders.

## Part 9. Virtual instruments

**Purpose.** Instruments that perform parts musically, not just play a sound.

**9.1 Asset specification.** An instrument MUST expose: pitch range; articulations; dynamics; timing and humanization; phrasing and expression curves; sound-design controls (tone, attack, space); and context inputs (the scene's harmony, tempo, density, and neighboring parts).

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 9. Virtual instruments
chunks.t:
controls (tone, attack, space); and context inputs (the scene's harmony, tempo, density, and neighboring parts).

**9.2 Performance behavior.** Given a part and context, the instrument produces a realistic performance, for example strummed versus fingerpicked guitar voicings, or a bass line that locks with the kick. It MUST render consistently across the whole song.

**9.3 Distillation workflow.**

1. Choose a teacher: a large model, a sampled library, or a synthesis pipeline.
2. Generate a broad, controlled set of performances across controls and contexts.
3. Train a smaller student for the target hardware tier.
4. Run a **loss audit** comparing student to teacher on timbre, range, articulation, expression, controllability, and latency.
5. Record the audit in the asset. Ship only if it clears thresholds.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 9. Virtual instruments
chunks.t:
expression, controllability, and latency.
5. Record the audit in the asset. Ship only if it clears thresholds.

**Acceptance tests.** The instrument performs unseen passages, not only training material. Controls produce monotonic, audible effects. The student-teacher audit is within tolerance. Draft-tier real-time factor meets target.

## Part 10. Audio-to-preset inverse rendering

**Purpose.** Treat a finished recording as evidence of a production setup, infer an editable preset, and apply it to new material.

**10.1 Pipeline.**

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 10. Audio-to-preset inverse rendering
chunks.t:
as evidence of a production setup, infer an editable preset, and apply it to new material.

**10.1 Pipeline.**

1. Analyze the reference: separate sources where possible, detect roles, measure tonal balance, dynamics, stereo image, space, and per-section changes.
2. Propose a structured preset.
3. Render the preset on the reference's own material and compare, to check fit.
4. Return the preset with alternatives and confidence.
5. Apply it to new material; the user listens, compares, and refines.

**10.2 Preset format.** An editable graph or parameterized recipe covering: instrument and source-role choices; arrangement and register tendencies; effects with order, parameters, and ranges; spatial, dynamic, and tonal targets; per-section automation and transition behavior. Not an opaque embedding.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 10. Audio-to-preset inverse rendering
chunks.t:
ranges; spatial, dynamic, and tonal targets; per-section automation and transition behavior. Not an opaque embedding.

**10.3 Honesty about ambiguity.** Different chains can produce similar audio. The system MUST return plausible presets with confidence and alternatives, and MUST NOT claim to recover the single true chain.

**Acceptance tests.** Self-fit: the preset rendered on the reference closely matches it. Transfer: producers judge that the preset applied to different songs and instrumentation captures the reference's character. Editability: changing one preset parameter changes the render predictably.

## Part 11. Artist profile

**Purpose.** A persistent, explainable model built from a creator's uploads that supplies context to every tool.

**11.1 Structure.** The profile has separate, inspectable dimensions. Each stores tendencies and ranges, not a recipe:

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 11. Artist profile
chunks.t:
Structure.** The profile has separate, inspectable dimensions. Each stores tendencies and ranges, not a recipe:

- **Musical identity:** harmony, melody shapes, rhythmic feel, phrasing, song structure.
- **Sound and arrangement:** instruments, roles, combinations, density, register, how parts enter and develop.
- **Performance:** vocal character, delivery, timing, dynamics, articulation, expressive range.
- **Production:** tonal balance, space, effects, stereo image, dynamics, automation habits.
- **Variation:** what changes by track, section, era, or mood.

Never collapse these into a single style vector.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 11. Artist profile
chunks.t:
**Variation:** what changes by track, section, era, or mood.

Never collapse these into a single style vector.

**11.2 Relationship graph.** Each upload gets a track-level analysis. A graph links tracks, sections, parts, performances, presets, and recurring traits. Every edge MUST point to audible evidence (a section, pattern, role, or feature), not only a similarity score. The system MUST be able to answer: what do these two tracks share; what makes this one an outlier; which traits recur in choruses but not verses; is the new demo closer to the sparse songs or the dense ones; which traits are probably specific to one recording.

**11.3 Modes.** If the artist has distinct modes (sparse versus dense, early versus recent), represent them as separate contexts. Do not blend them into an average. For a new project, offer three choices: follow a mode, combine modes, or explore away from them.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 11. Artist profile
chunks.t:
them into an average. For a new project, offer three choices: follow a mode, combine modes, or explore away from them.

**11.4 Explanations.** Every profile-driven suggestion MUST show its rationale and cite the uploads and sections it draws on. Example: "Close, dry vocal and sparse verse texture from tracks A and B; brighter chorus lift from track C."

**11.5 Corrections.** Users can mark a trait as specific to one track, keep a trait but drop another, combine traits from different uploads, or declare a new direction. A correction updates only the relevant dimension, is versioned, and can be rolled back. The profile keeps a visible history.

**11.6 Scope selection.** Every tool that uses the profile exposes a context selector: full catalog, chosen references, an era or mode, or none. The default is shown, never hidden.

**11.7 Where the profile is used.**

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 11. Artist profile
chunks.t:
chosen references, an era or mode, or none. The default is shown, never hidden.

**11.7 Where the profile is used.**

- Composition: structures, chords, melodies, and transitions consistent with selected references.
- Voice characters: preserve identity while the performance varies.
- Virtual instruments: choose parts, articulations, and registers that fit the artist's habits.
- Presets: reuse or adapt inferred chains without applying them indiscriminately.
- Arrangement assistance: suggest what to add, remove, or develop in the current section.
- Editing: make a local change while preserving the project's chosen direction.

**11.8 Privacy.** Profiles are private by default. Uploads and derived profile data are encrypted, exportable by the owner, and deletable with cascading removal of derived data. Profile data MUST NOT enter shared training sets without a separate, explicit opt-in.

chunks.h: Open Music Creation System: The Build Manual > Part 11. Artist profile
chunks.t:
removal of derived data. Profile data MUST NOT enter shared training sets without a separate, explicit opt-in.

**Acceptance tests.** The system explains why two uploads feel related with specific evidence and identifies meaningful differences. Carrying over a chosen subset of traits changes only those traits. Output with profile context on differs measurably from output with it off. Deleting an upload removes it and its derived traits.

## Part 12. Editing engine

**Purpose.** Editing is the central differentiator. Prompt-to-song with a full reroll is not enough.

**12.1 Operations.** The engine MUST support:

- **Inpainting:** replace a selected time range while preserving the surrounding audio.
- **Continuation:** extend an intro, section, or full track.
- **Section regeneration:** produce another verse or chorus without losing the song's identity.
- **Part and stem operations:** gene

- **Part and stem operations:** gene

rate, replace, extract, remove, or rebalance a vocal or instrument.
- **Arrangement edits:** add or remove an instrument, change density, shift the energy of a section.
- **Lyric edits:** change a line and realign the singing to the music.
- **Performance replacement:** re-perform one phrase or part with a different instruction.
- **Asset swap:** change the voice character, instrument, or preset and re-render affected elements.
- **Reference conditioning:** guide any of the above with a supplied melody, chord chart, performance, or sound palette.
- **Automation editing:** change a parameter curve and re-render only what it touches.

**12.2 Edit contract.** Every edit takes a scene version, a target selection (time range, part, or element), an instruction, and a lock set. It returns a new scene version, new audio for the affected elements, and an **edit report** listing what changed, what was kept, and which seeds and assets were used.

**12.3 Locality.** A targeted edit MUST mostly affect the requested area or element.

**12.3 Locality.** A targeted edit MUST mostly affect the requested area or element.

- Define an **edit mask** for each operation (time range and, where relevant, stem).
- Measure audio difference outside the mask with a perceptual distance. Set the threshold in Part 1.
- Measure seams at mask boundaries (clicks, level jumps, phase problems).
- Locked elements MUST be unchanged; state whether the guarantee is bit-exact or perceptual.
- Measure the intended change inside the mask against the instruction.

**12.4 Dependency-aware re-rendering.** Keep a dependency graph from scene elements to rendered audio. After an edit, re-render only nodes whose inputs changed, then re-run the mix. Show the user what will be re-rendered before an expensive operation.

nodes whose inputs changed, then re-run the mix. Show the user what will be re-rendered before an expensive operation.

**12.5 Takes.** Generate several alternatives on request, compare them side by side, and allow comping across takes. Every take is a version.

**Acceptance tests.** On the edit suite (Part 17), median outside-mask difference is below threshold; no audible seams in blinded checks; instruction success rate meets target for each operation; a lyric edit changes only the edited line and its immediate transitions.

**13.1 Mixer.** Applies levels, panning, tone, dynamics, space, buses, and automation from the production graph and scene. It MUST be deterministic given the same inputs. It MUST avoid clipping and report loudness and true-peak values.

**13.3 Export.** Provide:

- Mixed audio (WAV at 16 or 24 bit, 44.1 or 48 kHz) and common compressed formats.

## Part 15. Project state, versioning, and reproducibility

**15.1 Project bundle.** A project contains scenes and their version graph; pinned asset versions; seeds; render settings; cached audio linked to exact scene versions; and references to profile snapshots used.

**15.2 Pinning.** Record hashes of model weights, tokenizer, preset engine, and mixer for every render. A render MUST be reproducible from its recorded inputs.

**15.3 Reproducibility levels.** State per tier: *Level A*, bit-exact on pinned software and hardware; *Level B*, perceptually equivalent across hardware. Do not claim a level you have not tested.

**15.4 Migration.** The scene schema uses semantic versioning. Old projects MUST open in new releases through automated migration, with a report of any lossy step.

## Part 16. Training program

Train in stages. Each stage has an exit gate; do not start the next stage at scale until the gate is met. Instrumental generation, singing, and editing are separate quality challenges. Evaluate them independently before claiming general strength.

| Stage | Goal | Exit gate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Audio representation | Codec or latent space that keeps timbre, transients, stereo image, detail | Part 5 acceptance tests |
| 2. General music | Broad structure and sound across genres | Instrumental suite passes quality and structure thresholds |
| 3. Lyrics and vocals | Intelligible, aligned, expressive singing | Part 7 acceptance tests per language |
| 4. Conditioning | Follow scene, structure, controls, references, and edits | Instruction-following and locality thresholds |
| 5. Asset models | Voice encoder, instrument students, preset inference | Parts 8, 9, 10 acceptance tests |
| 6. Preference tuning | Improve musical usefulness using expert and user ratings | Blinded preference gain without regressions elsewhere |
| 7. Efficiency | Distill and optimize for Draft and Studio tiers | Latency and quality targets on each tier |

**Practices.**

- Run small-scale ablations before every large run. Record the decision each ablation informed.
- Evaluate checkpoints on the regression suite automatically; block promotion on regression.
- Store configs, data manifests, seeds, and code revisions with every checkpoint.
- Keep the preference data and its collection protocol versioned and auditable.
- Never tune on the test sets.

## Part 17. Evaluation program

Automatic metrics catch regressions. Professional quality requires listening.

**17.1 Fixed suite.** Build a frozen test suite across genres, languages, tempos, vocal types, song lengths, and prompt styles, plus a held-out hard set. Version it. Refresh on a published schedule without leaking into training.

**17.2 Human evaluation.** Run blinded comparisons with musicians, producers, vocalists, and ordinary listeners. Rate separately: prompt adherence, composition, vocal quality, coherence, production, and edit success. Report inter-rater agreement. Publish the protocol.

**17.3 Automatic checks.**

- Tempo and key accuracy; section timing.
- Lyric word error rate and alignment error.
- Loudness, clipping, silence, clicks, discontinuities, channel problems.
- Identity similarity for voice characters; timbre consistency across sections.
- Edit locality and boundary seams.
- Reproducibility.

**17.4 Transfer tests.** Test capabilities beyond the input that created them:

and boundary seams.

**17.4 Transfer tests.** Test capabilities beyond the input that created them:

- Does a voice character stay recognizable on new lyrics and melodies?
- Does an inferred preset work on a different song and instrumentation?
- Does a distilled instrument perform new passages, not only training examples?
- Can one asset change while the others stay stable?
- Do edits behave predictably across sections and full-length renders?

**17.5 Reliability.** Render every suite prompt across multiple seeds. Report the share of outputs passing all automatic checks and the rate of severe failures. **Purpose.** A professional system is more than a research notebook. Optimize the whole workflow (interpretation, generation, editing, mixing, download), not just raw model speed.

**18.1 Inference.** Efficient GPU inference with memory management, batching, and fast model loading. Apply quantization or distillation only where Part 17 tests show no unacceptable quality loss.

**18.2 Staged results.** Stream the sketch, then draft, then final, so users can decide before a full render finishes.

**18.3 Local and hosted.** Smaller models run locally on the Draft and Studio tiers. Larger models run hosted. The scene, assets, and project bundle move between them without conversion.

## Part 19. Consent, provenance, privacy, and safety

**Purpose.** These are engineering requirements with acceptance tests, not policy footnotes. The most sensitive capabilities in this system are voice characters and artist profiles built from other people's audio.

most sensitive capabilities in this system are voice characters and artist profiles built from other people's audio.

**19.1 Voice consent.** Implement Part 8.4 in full: recorded, verified consent tied to the person whose voice is used, or documented rights for a licensed or synthetic source. Block creation of a voice character of a named real person, including public figures, without that verification. Support owner revocation that takes effect for new renders immediately.

**19.2 Watermark and provenance.** Every render carries an inaudible watermark and signed provenance metadata that identifies the system, model versions, and project. Release a detection tool. State honestly how well the watermark survives common transformations (re-encoding, resampling, mild editing) and where it does not.

**19.3 Training data governance.** Use the Part 4 license ledger. Honor opt-outs and deletion requests. Do not train on user uploads or user-created assets by default; use a separate, explicit, revocable opt-in.

**19.4 User data.** Define retention. Provide owner export and deletion. Deletion cascades to derived assets, profile traits, caches, and backups on a stated schedule.

**19.5 Misuse handling.** Publish a usage policy. Provide a reporting and takedown channel. Detect and limit abuse patterns (bulk impersonation attempts, repeated consent failures) in ways that do not require listening to private projects.

**19.7 Legal review.** Assign counsel to review data sources, licensing, voice rights, and distribution for each jurisdiction you ship in. Version the policies the same way as code.

# Audio representation (Part 5)

A compressed representation that can be generated efficiently without losing
what musicians care about.

## Reference codec

`kindling.codec.FramedCodec` implements the `AudioCodec` interface in two
honest rates behind one contract:

chunks.h: Audio representation (Part 5) > Reference codec
chunks.t:
codec

`kindling.codec.FramedCodec` implements the `AudioCodec` interface in two
honest rates behind one contract:

- **draft**: 8-bit mu-law companded frames, 2:1 smaller than 16-bit PCM.
  Fast previews. Genuinely lossy (about 32 dB SNR on the test battery) with
  graceful degradation.
- **hifi**: 16-bit PCM frames, lossless (about 83 dB SNR, quantization only).

Both keep stereo (channels interleaved per frame), both decode isolated
regions (frames are independent, so a frame-aligned region reconstructs
bit-exactly), and both support multi-track token sets so separate parts can
be generated and replaced independently (stem-aware latents).

chunks.h: Audio representation (Part 5) > Reference codec
chunks.t:
both support multi-track token sets so separate parts can
be generated and replaced independently (stem-aware latents).

This is the reference implementation that establishes the interface and the
evaluation harness. Learned neural codecs plug into the same interface; the
bake-off in V6 judges renderers through it, and any codec can be swapped
without touching the rest of the system.

## Evaluation

`kindling.codec.eval.evaluate_codec()` runs the objective acceptance
battery on five signal categories (drums, vocals, solo piano, dense mix,
quiet material):

chunks.h: Audio representation (Part 5) > Evaluation
chunks.t:
runs the objective acceptance
battery on five signal categories (drums, vocals, solo piano, dense mix,
quiet material):

- **Spectral error**: mean log-spectral distance in dB, floor 100 dB below
  peak, counting only bins within 60 dB of each frame's peak (differences
  buried deeper are inaudible under the frame's own content).
- **Transient preservation**: surviving onset flux near each original onset.
- **Stereo correlation**: per-channel plus L-R difference correlation, which
  carries the stereo image.
- **Loudness drift**: worst windowed RMS level difference, skipping windows
  below -60 dBFS where the metric would measure quantization noise against
  silence instead of the codec.
- **Seam energy**: max sample difference where a region decode meets the
  full decode. Frame-aligned regions must be bit-exact.

chunks.h: Audio representation (Part 5) > Evaluation
chunks.t:
energy**: max sample difference where a region decode meets the
  full decode. Frame-aligned regions must be bit-exact.

Thresholds live in `THRESHOLDS` in the eval module, per rate. Both rates
pass the full battery. The listening half of the acceptance tests follows
`docs/listening-protocol.md` and is run by human panels, not CI.

# Data pipeline (Part 4)

Reproducible, traceable data with labels good enough to train structured,
editable models.

## Stages

chunks.h: Data pipeline (Part 4) > Stages
chunks.t:
(Part 4)

Reproducible, traceable data with labels good enough to train structured,
editable models.

## Stages

`kindling.data.Pipeline` runs every stage in order: ingest and validate,
normalize (canonical 48 kHz mono with a recorded loudness label), deduplicate
(exact sha256 plus a 512-bit perceptual fingerprint robust to small gain
changes), segment, analyze, separate (mid/side reference; the mix is always
kept), align lyrics from caller-provided transcripts, label instruments and
roles, score annotation quality, assign splits, write the record.

Analysis is classical DSP with numpy: onset-autocorrelation tempo, Krumhansl
key profiles, chroma-template chords, chroma-novelty sections, RMS energy,
and a spectral heuristic for instrument role. Every label carries a value,
a confidence, and the method that produced it.

## Honest boundaries

chunks.h: Data pipeline (Part 4) > Honest boundaries
chunks.t:
for instrument role. Every label carries a value,
a confidence, and the method that produced it.

## Honest boundaries

Three jobs need learned models that do not exist yet: lyric transcription
from audio, true source separation, and instrument classification. The
pipeline provides the interfaces and extension points for all three, plus
reference implementations whose limits are documented in the code: a
vocal-band onset aligner for provided transcripts, mid/side center
estimation, and a low-confidence spectral heuristic. Nothing is faked;
low-confidence labels are marked, not hidden, and training code can
threshold them.

## Records

chunks.h: Data pipeline (Part 4) > Records
chunks.t:
Nothing is faked;
low-confidence labels are marked, not hidden, and training code can
threshold them.

## Records

The per-track record (`kindling/data/record.py`, schema in code) stores the
content hash, source and acquisition method, license status and terms,
allowed uses, processing versions, every derived label with confidence,
split assignment, and a deletion handle.

## Rules, enforced in code

chunks.h: Data pipeline (Part 4) > Rules, enforced in code
chunks.t:
versions, every derived label with confidence,
split assignment, and a deletion handle.

## Rules, enforced in code

- Splits are fixed early and never leak. Assignment is deterministic from the
  content hash, and near-duplicates (including alternate mixes) are pinned to
  the original's split. `leakage_audit()` proves zero cross-split duplicates.
- Provenance is queryable: `LicenseLedger.by_source()`,
  `by_license_status()`, `by_allowed_use()`, `by_split()`.
- Deletion propagates: `delete_record()` excludes the item from every future
  manifest and lists derived assets for cascading removal where policy
  requires.
- Manifests (`build_manifest(pipeline, "train" | "evaluate")`) pin the
  processing versions so runs are reproducible.

## Rules encoded in records

- `license.status`: cleared, pending, restricted, unknown.

# Editing Engine (Part 12)

Editing is the central differentiator. Prompt-to-song with a full
reroll is not enough.

## Operations (12.1)

All ten, in `operations.py`, each deterministic given the seed:

chunks.h: Editing Engine (Part 12) > Operations (12.1)
chunks.t:
a full
reroll is not enough.

## Operations (12.1)

All ten, in `operations.py`, each deterministic given the seed:

- **inpaint**: replace notes in a time range with generated fill.
- **continue**: extend by N bars, carrying the last phrase forward.
- **regenerate_section**: rhythmic/velocity variation within a section,
  pitches kept (identity preserved).
- **part_stem**: generate, remove, or rebalance (quieter/louder) a part.
- **arrangement**: density up/down, section energy shifts.
- **lyric_edit**: change one line, flag for realignment.

# Functional milestone A: upload / save / use loop (V24)

Phase A wires the end-to-end loop in Python: upload your own audio, save it
as a versioned asset in an on-disk library, render a song from a prompt and
lyrics using those saved assets, download the results. Proven with real
audio, not fixtures.

## The loop

chunks.t:
a prompt and
lyrics using those saved assets, download the results. Proven with real
audio, not fixtures.

## The loop

```
kindling library upload track.wav --kind voice --name "Aries" \
    --consent-subject "Aries Hilton"
kindling library upload groove.wav --kind instrument --name "My Groove" \
    --role guitar
kindling library upload finished.wav --kind preset --name "My Chain"
kindling library list
kindling render --prompt "dark driving verse and chorus, 100 bpm" \
    --lyrics-file lyrics.txt --voice voice_aries \
    --instrument guitar=inst_my_groove --preset preset_my_chain \
    --seed 7 --out song/
kindling export song/ --format stems --out song-stems/
```

chunks.h: Functional milestone A: upload / save / use loop (V24) > The loop
chunks.t:
--preset preset_my_chain \
    --seed 7 --out song/
kindling export song/ --format stems --out song-stems/
```

The library lives at `~/.kindling/library` by default (`--library` overrides
it). Assets are JSON records; source audio is stored content-addressed
(sha256) under `audio/`. Deleting an asset removes its record and its audio
when no other asset references it.

## What each kind does

chunks.h: Functional milestone A: upload / save / use loop (V24) > What each kind does
chunks.t:
`audio/`. Deleting an asset removes its record and its audio
when no other asset references it.

## What each kind does

- **voice**: the reference is analyzed (pitch range, dynamics, registers,
  vowel states, sufficiency report) and saved as a voice character.
  Creating one requires a consent record: `--consent-subject NAME` for a
  personal voice, or `--rights-basis licensed|synthetic`. Rendering through
  the character checks consent, revocation, and per-performance sufficiency
  before any audio is made.
- **instrument**: the recording is sliced at detected onsets into a sample
  map with per-slice root pitch. At render time slices are pitched to the
  part's notes. Material with no stable pitch is marked unpitched and plays
  cyclically.
- **preset**: inverse rendering infers an editable effect graph from the
  finished track, with alternatives and confidence. The preset applies to
  the mix bus at render time.

## Honest boundaries of this milestone

- The vocal renderer is the reference procedural renderer: prosody and
  expressive-control path only, not an intelligible singing voice. A
  learned vocal model plugs into the same interface.
- Uploaded instruments are sample maps, not learned instruments.
- The preset chain is real DSP (shelves, compressor, delay, widener)
  inferred from measurements, with stated confidence and alternatives.
- Voice character `voice_aries` was built from a mastered full mix, not an
  isolated vocal, so its identity vector includes mix bleed. An a cappella
  reference would sharpen it later. This is recorded on the asset.

# Audio-to-Preset Inverse Rendering (Part 10)

Treat a finished recording as evidence of a production setup, infer an
editable preset, and apply it to new material.

## Pipeline (10.1)

chunks.h: Audio-to-Preset Inverse Rendering (Part 10) > Pipeline (10.1)
chunks.t:
as evidence of a production setup, infer an
editable preset, and apply it to new material.

## Pipeline (10.1)

1. **Analyze** (`analyze_reference`): tonal balance (5 bands), spectral
   centroid, crest factor, stereo correlation, side level, space ratio,
   per-section changes, detected roles (bass/drums/harmonic/bright_lead
   from spectral signatures).
2. **Propose** (`propose_preset`): lowshelf/highshelf from tonal tilt,
   compressor from crest factor, delay from space ratio, widener from
   stereo correlation.
3. **Self-fit**: render the preset on new material; features move toward
   the reference (tested).
4. **Return** (`inverse_render`): preset + 2 alternatives + confidence +
   the full analysis.
5. **Apply** (`render_preset`): run the chain on any new audio.

## Preset format (10.2)

chunks.h: Audio-to-Preset Inverse Rendering (Part 10) > Preset format (10.2)
chunks.t:
+
   the full analysis.
5. **Apply** (`render_preset`): run the chain on any new audio.

## Preset format (10.2)

JSON-serializable dict: `chain` (ordered effects with params),
`targets` (measured reference features), `roles`, `sections`. Every
parameter has a validated range (`EFFECT_SPECS`); `edit_preset`
changes one parameter and returns a new preset. Not an opaque
embedding: every value is human-readable and editable.

Effects (real DSP in `effects.py`): lowshelf, highshelf, compressor,
delay (space), widener.

## Honesty about ambiguity (10.3)

Different chains can produce similar audio. The pipeline returns
plausible presets with confidence and alternatives, and the result
carries an explicit disclaimer: "plausible inference; different chains
can produce similar audio". It NEVER claims to recover the single true
chain.

# Listening test protocol (Part 5 and Part 17)

Automated metrics catch regressions. Professional quality requires
listening. This protocol covers codec reconstruction (Part 5) and, later,
generation quality (Part 17).

## Panel

- Minimum 8 listeners: at least 3 working musicians, producers, or
  engineers, plus ordinary listeners.
- Blind: listeners never know which system or setting produced a sample.
- Calibrated playback: listeners confirm their monitoring chain before
  the session.

## Material

chunks.h: Listening test protocol (Part 5 and Part 17) > Material
chunks.t:
produced a sample.
- Calibrated playback: listeners confirm their monitoring chain before
  the session.

## Material

- Drums, vocals, solo piano, dense mixes, and quiet material (Part 5).
- Later: the fixed suite across genres, languages, tempos, vocal types,
  song lengths, and prompt styles (Part 17).

## Method

- ABX for artifact detection: can the listener tell the reconstruction
  from the original?
- MUSHRA-style rating for quality: rate each sample 0 to 100 on
  timbre, transients, stereo image, and overall quality.
- Report inter-rater agreement. Publish the protocol, the results, and
  representative failure cases, not only selected demos.

## Release use

A codec or model release passes only if it clears both the automated
battery (`kindling.codec.eval`, later `kindling.eval`) and this protocol's
thresholds from `targets.yaml`.

# Mix, Mastering, and Export (Part 13)

## Mixer (13.1)

`Mixer.mix(stems, production)`: applies levels, constant-power panning,
buses, and automation from the production graph. Deterministic given
the same inputs. Avoids clipping (limits to 0.99 and reports it).
Reports K-weighted loudness (LUFS-ish) and true peak (4x oversampled)
for the mix and per stem.

## Mastering stage (13.2)

`master(mix, rate, target, reference_lufs, bypass)`: optional and
separable. Loudness targets for streaming (-14), club (-9), broadcast
(-16), cinema (-20). Optional reference matching via `reference_lufs`.
`bypass=True` returns the mix untouched. The report ALWAYS lists what
was applied; mastering is never silent.

returns the mix untouched. The report ALWAYS lists what
was applied; mastering is never silent.

## Export (13.3)

`export_all`: 
- mix.wav (16/24-bit, 44.1/48 kHz with resampling),
- stems/ (time-aligned, loudness-labeled manifest),
- score.mid (from scene parts; None with an explicit note where no
  note-bearing parts exist),
- lyrics.lrc (timed lyrics),
- sidecar.json (scene, asset versions, seeds, render settings,

# Song planning and rendering (Part 6)

## Prompt interpreter (6.1)

`kindling.planning.interpret()` turns natural language, tags, lyrics, and
controls into a draft scene plus an assumptions list. It extracts tempo
("92 bpm"), key ("F# minor"), sections (verse, chorus, bridge, intro,
outro, pre-chorus), and mood words that bias energy, and records every
default it chose ("assumed 120 BPM (no tempo in prompt)") instead of hiding
it. The scene it returns is fully readable and editable.

## Composition planner (6.2)

chunks.h: Song planning and rendering (Part 6) > Composition planner (6.2)
chunks.t:
in prompt)") instead of hiding
it. The scene it returns is fully readable and editable.

## Composition planner (6.2)

`ReferencePlanner` proposes form, harmony, motifs, energy curve, and
arrangement from real functional harmony: per-section-type progressions in
the song's key and mode (for example C major verse: C - G - Am - F),
singable interval motifs on the song's scale, section-archetype energy
curves, and role assignments with entrances and exits per section.
`alternatives(scene, element, count)` offers variants of harmony, energy, or
motif. Locked elements are never touched by the planner.

## Renderer (6.3)

chunks.h: Song planning and rendering (Part 6) > Renderer (6.3)
chunks.t:
offers variants of harmony, energy, or
motif. Locked elements are never touched by the planner.

## Renderer (6.3)

`ReferenceRenderer` honors the stable interface: scene fragment in, audio
and metadata out. It renders deterministically with simple synthesis
(plucked, pad, and bass tones, noise-based drums, a soft guide tone for
vocal parts). The guide tone is honest about what it is: the metadata warns
that real vocal rendering is Part 7. Same seed and scene always give the
same audio.

The structured bake-off (`kindling.planning.bakeoff`) judges registered
renderers, autoregressive, parallel-latent, or planner-hybrid, against the
Part 1 targets, not demos: validity, determinism, coherence pass rate, and
cost. The reference renderer runs as the baseline every learned renderer
must beat, and the winner can replace it without touching the interface.

## Hierarchical generation (6.4)

chunks.h: Song planning and rendering (Part 6) > Hierarchical generation (6.4)
chunks.t:
renderer
must beat, and the winner can replace it without touching the interface.

## Hierarchical generation (6.4)

`HierarchicalRenderer` plans at song level, refines at section level, and
renders at chunk level. Chunks are 4-bar windows with 1-bar overlap, rebased
so each chunk starts at bar 1 beat 0. Every chunk is rendered with its
surrounding context: the previous chunk's tail audio and the next chunk's
scene, both passed in and recorded. Overlaps join with an equal-power
crossfade, so chunk boundaries do not click.

## Long-form coherence (6.5)

chunks.h: Song planning and rendering (Part 6) > Long-form coherence (6.5)
chunks.t:
recorded. Overlaps join with an equal-power
crossfade, so chunk boundaries do not click.

## Long-form coherence (6.5)

`coherence_report(scene, audio, rate)` runs the automatic checks: tempo
drift per section against the tempo map, key violations per section against
the key map, lyric completeness (every line referenced), motif return (the
planner's motif intervals recurring in the melody), and intentional
transitions (arrangement changes or explicit transition marks at every
boundary; unmarked boundaries are warnings).

## Preview tiers (6.6)

Sketch (first 8 seconds at low rate, lowest cost), draft (full song, good
enough for decisions), final (full quality). Rendering is deterministic, so
a change heard in the sketch predicts the change in the final.

# Project State, Versioning, and Reproducibility (Part 15)

## Project bundle (15.1)

`ProjectBundle`: scenes + version graph (child -> parents), pinned
asset versions, seeds, render settings, cached audio linked to exact
scene versions, and profile snapshots. Saves to `project.json` with a
SHA256 integrity manifest; `verify_integrity` checks it on load.

## Pinning (15.2)

`pin_render_inputs()`: SHA256 of the renderer, mixer, preset engine,
and tokenizer source plus the Kindling version, recorded for every
render. A render MUST be reproducible from its recorded inputs.

## Reproducibility levels (15.3)

chunks.h: Project State, Versioning, and Reproducibility (Part 15) > Reproducibility levels (15.3)
chunks.t:
recorded for every
render. A render MUST be reproducible from its recorded inputs.

## Reproducibility levels (15.3)

`check_reproducibility(before, after, rate)`:
- **Level A**: bit-exact (sample-identical).
- **Level B**: perceptually equivalent (< 1 dB gated spectral distance).
- Otherwise: no level claimed, with an explicit note not to claim
  reproducibility.

The reference deterministic renderer achieves Level A on pinned
software; Level B is the honest claim across hardware. Never claim a
level you have not tested.

## Migration (15.4)

Scene schema uses semantic versioning (current 3.0.0).
`migrate_scene` walks 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0 -> 3.0.0 automatically and
returns every lossy step (default meta inserted, estimated lyric
timing, initialized automation/routing). Zero unreported loss: if it
is not in the `lossy` list, it did not happen.

`embed_watermark`: 64-bit spread-spectrum mark in the 2-4 kHz band

# The Musical Scene (Part 3)

One shared representation connecting intent, symbolic music, performance,
and audio. The scene is the source of truth; rendered audio is derived and
can always be regenerated from the scene, assets, seeds, and settings.

## Format

The open, documented format is `kindling/scene/scene.schema.json`
(JSON Schema, draft 2020-12). Scenes are plain dicts validated against it,
so the in-memory format and the on-disk format are the same thing.

chunks.h: The Musical Scene (Part 3) > Format
chunks.t:
Scenes are plain dicts validated against it,
so the in-memory format and the on-disk format are the same thing.

A scene holds: timeline (tempo, meter, and key maps plus section boundaries
in bars and seconds), sections, harmony, melody, lyrics, parts, vocal parts,
automation lanes, the production graph, render settings, and provenance.

Every element carries metadata: `source` (user, planner, inferred,
imported), `confidence` (0 to 1), `locked` (the system must not change it),
and `realization` (intent, symbolic, performance, audio). Partially realized
scenes are valid: a section can exist as an intent ("bigger second chorus")
long before it has notes.

Asset references are content-addressed: `{"id", "version", "sha256"}`,
displayed as `id@version`.

## Store

`kindling.scene.SceneStore` implements the interface contract:

## Store

`kindling.scene.SceneStore` implements the interface contract:

- Immutable versions. Version ids are the sha256 of the canonical scene
  JSON, so identical scenes always get identical ids. Loading returns a
  copy; nothing stored is ever mutated.
- Branches and full parent history.
- Human-readable element-level diffs, for example
  `chorus (sec_chorus2): energy 0.6 -> 0.8` or `added part 'pad' (role: pad)`.
- Three-way merges with conflict reporting. Conflicts are reported with
  both values, never silently resolved.

## Import and export

chunks.h: The Musical Scene (Part 3) > Import and export
chunks.t:
with conflict reporting. Conflicts are reported with
  both values, never silently resolved.

## Import and export

- MIDI: `kindling.scene.midi` reads and writes real MIDI files (format 0/1,
  note on/off, tempo map, time signature, track names). Round-trip keeps
  every note: pitch, start, duration, velocity.
- MusicXML: `kindling.scene.musicxml_io` reads and writes score-partwise
  files for the subset the scene needs.
- Finished audio and stems: `kindling.scene.audio_import` analyzes WAV
  files deterministically (duration, peak, RMS, onset-based tempo estimate
  with confidence, per-second energy curve) and imports them as
  audio-realization elements. Structural content is marked as not yet
  analyzed, with a warning, instead of being invented. The reference
  analyzer (V6) and preset inference (V10) build on this.

## Acceptance

- MIDI round-trip with no note loss: tested.
- Saved scene re-render reproducibility: version ids are deterministic;

- Edit one section, diff lists only that section's elements: tested.

# Training Program (Part 16)

Train in stages. Each stage has an exit gate; do not start the next
stage at scale until the gate is met.

## Stages

chunks.h: Training Program (Part 16) > Stages
chunks.t:
in stages. Each stage has an exit gate; do not start the next
stage at scale until the gate is met.

## Stages

| # | Stage | Exit gate |
|---|-------|-----------|
| 1 | Audio representation | Codec spectral error < 3 dB on test signals |
| 2 | General music | Reference bakeoff passes (the bar to beat) |
| 3 | Lyrics and vocals | Part 7 acceptance per language |
| 4 | Conditioning | Instruction-following and locality thresholds |
| 5 | Asset models | Parts 8/9/10 acceptance (distillation audit) |
| 6 | Preference tuning | Blinded preference gain, no regressions |
| 7 | Efficiency | Real-time factor <= 1.0 on Draft/Studio tiers |

`check_all_stages` runs gates in order and stops at the first failure,
naming the blocked stage. Instrumental generation, singing, and
editing are evaluated independently before any claim of general
strength.

## Practices (enforced in code)

## Practices (enforced in code)

- **Ablations**: `Ablation` runs small-scale variants and records the
  decision each one informed.
- **Checkpoints**: `Checkpoint` stores config, data manifest, seeds,
  and code revision. `RegressionSuite.evaluate` blocks promotion on
  any regression.
- **Preference data**: versioned and auditable (protocol in Part 17).
- **Never tune on test sets**: `TestSetGuard` hashes test IDs and
  refuses `train` purpose on them.

## Honest status

No models are trained yet. This part builds the program: the stages,
the gates, and the practices as runnable infrastructure. When training
begins, it runs through these gates; until then the gates run against
the reference implementations.

# Virtual Instruments (Part 9)

Instruments that perform parts musically, not just play a sound. Given
a part and context, the instrument makes musical decisions: articulation,
timing, dynamics, phrasing. It renders consistently across the whole song.

## The asset (9.1)

`InstrumentAsset` MUST expose: pitch range, articulations, dynamics,
timing/humanization, phrasing/expression curves, sound-design controls
(tone, attack, space) with min/max/default, and context inputs (harmony,
tempo, density, neighboring parts). `validate()` returns spec violations.

Reference assets: `kindling-guitar` (strummed/fingerpicked/muted/
harmonic), `kindling-bass` (fingered/picked/slap/muted),
`kindling-keys` (sustained/staccato/tremolo).

## Performance behavior (9.2)

chunks.h: Virtual Instruments (Part 9) > Performance behavior (9.2)
chunks.t:
(fingered/picked/slap/muted),
`kindling-keys` (sustained/staccato/tremolo).

## Performance behavior (9.2)

`PerformanceEngine.perform(part, context, instrument, seed)`:

- **Guitar**: dense context -> strummed voicings with strum spread;
  sparse context -> fingerpicked. Downbeats accented, phrases shaped
  with a slight crescendo.
- **Bass**: locks note starts to the kick pattern from context
  neighbors (within 0.25 beats). Picks articulation by density.
- **All**: timing humanization (seeded Gaussian jitter), deterministic:
  same part + same seed = same performance, so the song renders
  consistently.

## Distillation workflow (9.3)

`distill_guitar()` / `distill_bass()` implement the five steps:

chunks.h: Virtual Instruments (Part 9) > Distillation workflow (9.3)
chunks.t:
consistently.

## Distillation workflow (9.3)

`distill_guitar()` / `distill_bass()` implement the five steps:

1. **Teacher**: high-detail reference synth (Karplus-Strong with rich
   excitation; 16-partial filtered saw bass).
2. **Distillation set**: broad, controlled performances across notes
   and controls (tone/attack/space).
3. **Student**: same interface, cheaper (single-period excitation;
   6 partials). Free parameters fitted by grid search.
4. **Loss audit** on held-out (unseen) passages: spectral distance,
   onset attack match, real-time factor, control monotonicity.
5. **Record**: the audit dict goes in the asset; `passes` is True only
   if all thresholds clear.

Thresholds: 6 dB spectral distance, 8 ms attack diff, real-time factor
<= 1.0, monotonic tone->brightness. These are the reference
tolerances; tighten them as the synths improve.

chunks.h: Virtual Instruments (Part 9) > What is interface vs implementation
chunks.t:
factor
<= 1.0, monotonic tone->brightness. These are the reference
tolerances; tighten them as the synths improve.

## What is interface vs implementation

- **Real**: the asset spec, the performance engine's musical decisions,
  the distillation workflow, the loss audit, the determinism guarantees.
- **Reference**: teacher and student are procedural DSP, not neural
  networks. A trained student would replace the parametric fit in step
  3 behind the same interface; the audit is model-agnostic.
- **Honest**: the student is simpler by construction; the audit measures
  the gap instead of hiding it.

# Vocal separation (classical DSP)

`kindling/assets/separate.py` splits a finished mix into a vocal estimate
and an accompaniment estimate with classical DSP only: numpy and scipy,
no learned models, no downloaded weights, no GPU, deterministic. It exists
for one job: cleaning reference audio before voice analysis, so a voice
character's identity vector carries less bleed from the beat.

## How it works

Two cues, combined per time-frequency bin (STFT, 2048-point Hann, 75%
overlap):

chunks.h: Vocal separation (classical DSP) > How it works
chunks.t:
bleed from the beat.

## How it works

Two cues, combined per time-frequency bin (STFT, 2048-point Hann, 75%
overlap):

1. **Center channel.** In mastered mixes the lead vocal sits panned
   center. Each bin scores centeredness from the mid/side power ratio,
   softly sharpened. Wide-panned content scores near zero.
2. **Repeating background (REPET-style).** Loop-based accompaniment
   repeats; the vocal does not. The loop period comes from autocorrelation
   of the 40-150 Hz kick-band energy envelope: the kick repeats with the
   beat and the voice lives above it, so the beat's repetition survives
   even when a loud vocal dominates the broadband envelope. The repeating
   spectrogram is the element-wise median across whole periods; bins that
   match it are accompaniment.

chunks.h: Vocal separation (classical DSP) > How it works
chunks.t:
The repeating
   spectrogram is the element-wise median across whole periods; bins that
   match it are accompaniment.

A bin must look both centered and non-repeating to count as vocal. That
is the whole trick: kick and bass are centered but they repeat, so the
repetition cue rejects them; wide hats and stereo instruments may not
repeat in place, but the center cue rejects them.

`separate_vocals(audio, sample_rate)` takes mono `(N,)` or stereo
`(2, N)` and returns `(vocal, accompaniment)` in the same layout, with
sample counts preserved exactly. The two estimates sum back to the
mixture.

## Use in voice analysis

chunks.h: Vocal separation (classical DSP) > Use in voice analysis
chunks.t:
same layout, with
sample counts preserved exactly. The two estimates sum back to the
mixture.

## Use in voice analysis

`analyze_reference(..., separate_vocals=False)` keeps its default
behavior exactly. With `separate_vocals=True` (and `stereo=...`), the
vocal is isolated first, mixed to mono, conditioned with a 120 Hz
highpass against residual kick and bass rumble, then analyzed. The
summary records the separation under `"separation"` so provenance always
shows how a reference was made.

## Measured performance

On synthetic mixtures with known ground truth (vocal-like harmonic line
with vibrato over a tiled 2 s drum/bass loop, `tests/test_separate.py`):

chunks.h: Vocal separation (classical DSP) > Measured performance
chunks.t:
known ground truth (vocal-like harmonic line
with vibrato over a tiled 2 s drum/bass loop, `tests/test_separate.py`):

- Vocal SDR: 7.2 dB (mixture) to 26.0 dB, +18.7 dB
- Vocal SIR: 7.2 dB to 30.9 dB, +23.6 dB
- Accompaniment SDR: -7.2 dB to 19.4 dB, +26.6 dB
- Spectral centroid of the analysis: 1334 Hz mixed, 1132 Hz separated,
  846 Hz true vocal. The bleed is reduced, not gone.

## Honest limits

chunks.h: Vocal separation (classical DSP) > Honest limits
chunks.t:
the analysis: 1334 Hz mixed, 1132 Hz separated,
  846 Hz true vocal. The bleed is reduced, not gone.

## Honest limits

- Works best on centered vocals over repetitive beats. That is the shape
  of a loop-built catalog, which is why this method was chosen.
- Residual bleed remains on wide-panned ad-libs, heavy vocal reverb
  tails, and anything the accompaniment does once and never repeats.
- Very short clips (under a few loop repetitions) fall back to a global
  median background; quality degrades gracefully, not silently.
- It is a bleed reducer for reference analysis, not a studio stem
  splitter. A learned separator would win on difficult material; this
  one wins on zero cost, zero weights, and running anywhere.

# Vocals and lyrics (Part 7)

Vocals are the hardest quality challenge, so they are their own system.

## Pronunciation (per-language G2P)

`kindling.vocals.g2p` phonemizes text into syllables with phonemes and
stress. Supported languages, tested separately and listed explicitly:

chunks.h: Vocals and lyrics (Part 7) > Pronunciation (per-language G2P)
chunks.t:
phonemizes text into syllables with phonemes and
stress. Supported languages, tested separately and listed explicitly:

- **en**: English. Letter-to-sound rules with an exception lexicon,
  syllabification, stress heuristics, and elision ("every" is two
  syllables).
- **es**: Spanish. Near-phonetic mapping with real stress rules, including
  accent-marked stress and diphthong handling.

Any other language raises instead of guessing. Learned G2P models plug into
the `Phonemizer` interface.

## Alignment

`align_line()` aligns syllables to melody notes at syllable level: one
syllable per note normally, melisma when notes outnumber syllables, and
explicit unassigned status (with a warning, never silent) when syllables
outnumber notes. Every alignment carries a confidence.

## Expressive controls

chunks.h: Vocals and lyrics (Part 7) > Expressive controls
chunks.t:
a warning, never silent) when syllables
outnumber notes. Every alignment carries a confidence.

## Expressive controls

`validate_performance()` covers all required controls: dynamics,
breathiness, vibrato rate and depth, belt, whisper, phrasing legato,
timing push/lay-back, doubles, and harmonies. Unknown or out-of-range
values raise instead of degrading silently.

## Reference vocal renderer

`ReferenceVocalRenderer` renders one lyric line deterministically: vowels
are harmonic tones with vibrato, fricatives are shaped noise, stops are
bursts, and every expressive control audibly changes the output. It is
honest about its limits in its own metadata: prosody and control path
only, not an intelligible singing voice. A learned singing model plugs
into the `VocalRenderer` interface.

## Line-level regeneration

chunks.h: Vocals and lyrics (Part 7) > Line-level regeneration
chunks.t:
singing voice. A learned singing model plugs
into the `VocalRenderer` interface.

## Line-level regeneration

`regenerate_line()` changes one lyric line: re-phonemize, re-align to the
line's notes, re-render only that line. The scene carries the new text and
alignment, the returned audio covers exactly the line's time range, and
every other line is listed as unchanged. Part 12 generalizes this into the
editing engine.

chunks.t:
and
every other line is listed as unchanged. Part 12 generalizes this into the

## Intelligibility

- `word_error_rate()` is the real WER computation.
- `TranscriptionModel` is the ASR interface; `wer_report()` runs the true
  acceptance path (transcribe, then score) and refuses to invent a
  transcript without a model.
- `ReferenceIntelligibility` runs deterministic proxy checks (syllable
  onset count, voicing ratio) and flags lines below threshold. Every report
  states it is a proxy. It flags the reference renderer's output, which is
  the system working as intended.
